name: Ankiya Nat and Bhaona
tagline: One-act plays of Sankardeva, played with song, drums and giant masks.
facts: Ankiya Nat: one-act plays in Brajavali, credited to Srimanta Sankardeva
Bhaona is the staging of an Ankiya Nat
Narrator: the sutradhar; musicians: gayan-bayan
Masks come in three sizes: mukha, lutukai, bor-mukha
art: Ankiya Nat are one-act plays from Assam. Wikipedia says their invention is usually attributed to the medieval saint and reformer Srimanta Sankardeva. They are written in Brajavali, a stylised poetic language, and mainly honour Krishna. A bhaona is a staging of an Ankiya Nat, with live instruments, singers, dance and elaborate costumes.

A performance has a set order. It opens with a Sanskrit benediction and a hymn in Brajavali. Then comes the purvaranga, a prelude by the gayan-bayan pair, the singer and the musician, with percussion and large cymbals. The sutradhar, a narrator, then carries the play forward. He directs, comments on the drama and explains each stage, since audiences were not expected to read.

Masks are an important part. Garland magazine says there are loukik masks (worldly figures such as humans and animals) and aloukik masks (otherworldly figures such as demons and demigods), in three sizes: mukha (face only), lutukai (face and chest) and bor-mukha (head and body). Makers use bamboo, wood, cloth, clay and cow dung, painted with vegetable dyes. The masks are said to be believed to be animate, so they are kept in the namghar and worshipped before and after a show.
Stories come from the Mahabharata, Ramayana and Bhagavata Purana. Performances once lasted through the night and now often last a few hours.
artist: Bhaona is a community act of devotion. Monks of the sattras, called bhokots, and village players take the roles. Sattriya dance was created as part of bhaona, according to Wikipedia's Sattriya article, and traditionally only male monks performed.

Mask makers are artists in their own right. Garland magazine profiles Hem Chandra Goswami, head of the Notun Samaguri sattra on Majuli, who says he descends from the original Goswami khanikars, or mask makers. It says five of his works are in the British Museum's permanent collection.
Sahapedia describes mask making as about 500 years old and says it began in the sattras, where Sankardeva taught masks to his followers as a way to spread his teaching through entertainment.
place: Majuli, a river island in the Brahmaputra, is the best known home of mask making and sattra life. The Notun Samaguri sattra there, founded around 1663 by Ahom king Chakradhwaj Singha according to Garland, is a major hub for mask production.
Garland counts over 800 sattras in Assam today. Bhaona is staged in their namghars, the congregation halls, and in village namghars across the state.

history.what: Sankardeva, saint, poet and reformer, creates the Ankiya Nat and founds the sattra and namghar tradition. Sources differ on his dates; Sahapedia says fifteenth century and Garland says sixteenth.
Some sources say Sankardeva made the first masks for his play Cihna Yatra in 1468. This date is traditional and is not confirmed by the sources we read.
Notun Samaguri sattra on Majuli is founded and becomes a centre for mask making.
The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises Sattriya, which grew with bhaona, as a classical dance.

future: Training: keep teaching bhaona to boys and girls in the sattras and village namghars.
Livelihood: mask makers need steady orders from sattras, museums and schools, not only gallery sales.
Materials: bamboo, clay and natural dyes should stay in use, as Garland notes a shift to synthetic paints.
Documentation: record complete plays, tunes and mask-making steps with sattra elders.
Protection: masks are damaged by insects and weather, so safe storage and repair in the namghar matter.

name: Bhand Pather
tagline: Open-air satire from the Valley: one troupe, no fixed script, and plenty of laughter at the powerful.
facts: Folk theatre of Kashmir, played outdoors
No fixed script; passed on orally
Music live: dhol, nagara and surnai
Over 80 troupes once; about 15 active (one report)
art: Bhand Pather is the folk theatre of Kashmir. It is satirical, mixing drama, dance and music to comment on customs, wrongs and current events. The name joins Bhand, a satirical character and performer, with Pather, the word for the plays.

The J&K Arts Foundation says it is played outdoors, with the audience seated on the ground. There is no fixed script. The art is handed down by word of mouth in the guru-shishya way, so each show changes with the place and the people watching.
The performers act, dance and play music live, with no recorded sound. The accompaniment is dhol, nagara and surnai. The Foundation also lists a wooden flute, the pather, with a bell-shaped end.

Plays take up real subjects. The Foundation lists Raaze Pather on lavish rulers, Gosain Pather on the power of religious leaders, Chakdar Pather on the exploitation of farmers, Angreez Pather on the British, Bakarwal Pather on the exploitation of the Bakarwal shepherd community, and Haanz Pather on boatmen and tourists.
artist: The Bhands are a community of performers, and the art runs in families. The Foundation names Manzoor ul Haq, a seventh-generation Bhand from Budgam, who has performed across India and abroad and received a national award in 2010.
Performers are men, and men play the women's roles, the same page says. A single performer acts, dances and plays music.
Many have not taught their children the art, the Foundation reports, as artists blame government indifference. M. K. Raina of the National School of Drama has led efforts to revive the form.
place: The Foundation calls Wathora, in Budgam district, the centre of Bhand Pather, and says many families there still practise it. Performers have also come from other villages across the Valley.
Traditionally the plays were part of Eid celebrations and weddings and were played in open ground among villagers, which gave the form its closeness to the audience.

history.what: The Foundation calls the form centuries old. We did not find a source we could open that settles when or from where it came, so we give no date.
The art is passed on in families by word of mouth, which is why the repertoire changed with each age, with plays about rulers, the British, farmers and tourists.
Cinema, radio, television, the conflict in Kashmir and later digital media cut into its audience, the Foundation says.

The Foundation reports that over 80 Bhand theatres once operated, but only about 15 remain active. Government scholarships and a five-day workshop in Patnitop have been announced, and social media videos have brought new attention.

future: Training: fund the guru-shishya line with scholarships for young performers, as announced. Make sure the money reaches families.
Livelihood: pay troupes for festival and school shows, so artists can stay in the work.
Materials: support makers and players of the surnai, nagara and dhol that the form depends on.
Documentation: record the plays, songs and the senior Bhands, since the art has no written script.
Protection: keep the satire free and rooted in the villages, while sharing it in new settings.

name: Bhavai
tagline: Open-air night theatre of skits, satire and a long copper horn.
facts: Form: folk theatre made of short skits called vesha
Traditionally credited to Asait Thakar, 14th century
Performed by the Bhavaiyya community, with a long copper horn called bhungal
Said to be about 700 years old
art: Bhavai is a folk theatre of Gujarat made of short skits called vesha. Sahapedia says performances are in the open air and run through the night. Each night traditionally opens with a Ganpati no vesh.

Wikipedia says the troupe chief, the Nayak, opens with prayers, followed by appearances of Ganesha, Kali and a Brahmin before the vesh begins. The Nayak and a jester stay on stage to comment. Humour is the main mood, and the jester pair Rangalo and Rangli are favourites. Male actors play female roles.

Sahapedia sorts vesha into historical, religious, social-satire and skill-based acts. It says songs use six basic rhythms. Instruments include the tabla, kansijoda, jhanjh, sarangi and harmonium, and the bhungal, a long copper horn unique to Bhavai, which announces important characters and scene changes.
artist: Sahapedia says the Bhavaiyya community, also called Vyas or Nayak, held the claim to Bhavai, and its men were the sole performers for most of its history. Wikipedia adds regional names: Nayak in Mehsana, Bhojak in Kutch and Vyas in Saurashtra. Boys began training around age eight, starting as helpers.

Tradition credits Asait Thakar, a 14th-century Brahmin from Unjha, as its father. By Sahapedia's account, he rescued a headman's daughter, broke caste rules, was ostracised and began writing satirical plays. He is said to have composed about 360 vesha, of which around 60 survive. This is tradition, not documented history.
Wikipedia names Muljibhai Nayak, Pransukh Nayak and Chimanlal Naik as prominent 20th-century performers. Today actors from other backgrounds also perform, though Sahapedia says some purists object.
place: Bhavai belongs to the villages of north Gujarat. Troupes travel each year to patron villages and perform in the village square, called chanchar. The village temple often serves as the make-up room.

Wikipedia says it is partly a ritual offering to the goddess Amba, and is often performed at the Ambaji temple during Navratri. The Gujarat government opened a Bhavai training centre at Visnagar in the early 1980s, according to Sahapedia, and the Darpana Academy in Ahmedabad also trains actors.

history.what: Asait Thakar is credited with creating Bhavai. Scholars think it grew from earlier open-air folk entertainment.
Troupes were supported by village patronage. Wikipedia says patronage grew from land and support Asait received.
Muljibhai Nayak, Pransukh Nayak and Chimanlal Naik are named as prominent performers.
A state training centre starts at Visnagar.
Sahapedia says the form has declined as modern entertainment reached villages, and has seen some revival in urban theatre and NGO campaigns.

future: Training: support the Visnagar centre and troupes who teach boys and now girls.
Livelihood: steady village bookings and fair fees, since young people are leaving the profession.
Materials: keep bhungal makers and players, as few players remain.
Documentation: record the surviving vesha, music and rhythms with the troupes.
Protection: we found no official heritage listing; check with Sangeet Natak Akademi.

name: Bidesia
tagline: A Bhojpuri folk play about the man who went to the city and the wife who waited.
facts: Named after the play Bidesiya by Bhikhari Thakur (1887-1971)
Play first staged in 1912, published in 1917
Themes: migration, poverty, women's suffering
Women's roles traditionally played by men
art: Bidesia is a folk theatre of the Bhojpuri-speaking region. The name comes from Thakur's best-known play, Bidesiya, meaning the one who has gone abroad. Wikipedia gives the story: Bidesiya leaves for Calcutta to earn and does not return for years. His wife Pyari Sundari waits. A traveller carries her message to him and finds he has married again. He returns home, and she in the end accepts the second wife.

The show follows a pattern. The Theatre Times says it opens with a mangalacharan, a prayer, and a sutradhar, the narrator, introduces the story. A comic figure, Labaar, comes between scenes. The songs use folk rhythms and verse forms and are mostly sung. Characters stand for types: the migrant husband, the messenger, the faithful wife.

It was staged on a raised platform with the audience on three sides, lit by lanterns. Men played the women's roles, wearing long false hair and ornaments. The Theatre Times says Thakur drew on jatra, Ramlila, Raslila and Parsi theatre, and sometimes improvised on stage.
artist: Bhikhari Thakur (1887-1971) was from Kutubpur in Saran district. The Theatre Times says he came from a barber (nayi) family and was largely unschooled, but taught himself to read. He was playwright, singer, actor and leader of his troupe, and wrote many books, including Bidesia, Beti-Viyog and Vidhva-Vilap. He is often called the Shakespeare of Bhojpuri, a title attributed to Dr. Manoranjan Prasad Sinha.

Newslaundry reports that a few members of Thakur's troupe lived to be filmed, and that Ramchandra Manjhi, a veteran of this tradition, was to be honoured with the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award. Performers there said they had worked for 50 to 60 years without rehearsal.

Jainendra Dosta, who writes and directs on Thakur's life, told Newslaundry that city versions often cut the dance and songs and change the tunes. He also objects to the term Launda Naach for the form, saying it carries caste and sexual overtones.
place: The tradition belongs to the Bhojpuri region, which includes western Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Thakur's village, Kutubpur, is in Saran district on the Ganga and Ghaghara plain, near Chhapra.

Migration is the heart of the story. Many men from this area went to Calcutta and later to Assam and overseas. The Theatre Times says Bidesia travelled with migrants to places such as Fiji, Mauritius and Trinidad.

history.what: Bhikhari Thakur is born, per The Theatre Times.
The play Bidesiya (first published as Kaljug Bahar, later Bahara Bahar) is composed and staged, per Wikipedia. Details differ between sources.
The play is published as a book.
A Bhojpuri film Bidesiya is made from it, per Wikipedia.
Thakur dies.
Sangeet Natak Akademi honours for veterans of this tradition. Sources give different years.
Revivals and a play about Thakur's life are staged. Newslaundry reports concern over changes made for city audiences.

future: Training: repertory training for young actors and singers, in the Bhojpuri idiom
Livelihood: regular paid shows, not only festival nights
Materials: keep the song, dance and dialogue together, not only the plot
Documentation: record Thakur's songs and older troupe members, since his works live mostly through performance
Protection: respect the community's voice in how the form is named and staged

name: Bommalattam
tagline: Heavy wooden marionettes with up to twelve strings, now carried by a very few hands.
facts: Form: string puppet theatre (marionettes)
Stories: Ramayana, Mahabharata, Puranas and local legends
Older puppets were nearly life-sized and very heavy
The full twelve-string technique is nearly lost
art: Bommalattam comes from bommai (doll) and attam (play or dance). Sahapedia describes it as a form of Tamil puppetry that is now barely alive in a few regions because of film, television and the internet.

Sahapedia's article on the art says wood was chosen to suit the character. Sandalwood was used for Rama, Vishnu and Vinayaka, ebony and tamarind for rakshasas, red sandalwood for goddesses, and cheaper wood for ordinary people. Early puppets were nearly life-sized and carving one could take up to six months. Tanjore-style puppets have no legs, and the puppeteer Kudanthai Chandher borrowed the long Kathakali skirt to hide them.

Shows open with prayers to Shiva and Ganesha. A curtain stretched on poles hides the puppeteer. Older shows were called Sangeetha Bommalattam and used a harmonium and mridangam, and puppeteers wore waist bells so that their movements followed the rhythm. Puppets were once worked with twelve strings, which let the puppeteer move every part of the body.
Stories come from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas. Sahapedia names Valli Kalyanam, Harichandra, Lava Kusa, Nallatangal Kathai and Markadeyan Kathai. Chandher has also staged topical stories.
artist: Kumbakonam Mani Iyyer, called Bommalatta Bhoopathy, is named as having popularised the art and taught many disciples. Troupes named in the Sahapedia article include Mangala Gana Sabha, the Mayavaram Gananadar Nataka Sabha, and the Murugan Bommalatta Sabha, which has branches in Kumbakonam and Mayiladuthurai.

The article says the twelve-string method was lost when masters died without passing it on. It names Sankaranathan, a Padma Shri recipient, as the only remaining practitioner of the full technique, but ailing at the time of writing. His son Murugan runs a troupe at Mayiladuthurai.

Kudanthai Chandher began puppetry in 1970 after working as a stand-up comedian and poet. He now makes lighter glove puppets and cheap puppets from bottles, which are easy to carry, and trains a few young people. He told the writer that his own son is not interested.
place: Sahapedia calls Tamil Nadu the main hub of Bommalattam. The places it names in the story of the art are Tanjore district, Kumbakonam, Mayavaram and Mayiladuthurai in the Kaveri delta, and Dharmapuri district to the north-west, where a heavier form called katta bommalattam is known.
Performances take place in temples during festivals. Sahapedia says they can run seven to ten days and often go past midnight.
The delta towns are also where temple sculptors, the sthapathis, work. Puppeteers who cannot carve depend on them, which slows making because they work only between temple commissions.

history.what: Sahapedia says the art is believed to be about 4,000 years old. This is a tradition, not a documented date. It cites the Thirukkural, which uses puppets moved by strings as an image, and the Silappadikaram, which mentions Pavai Koothu.
The article says the earliest puppets were wooden dolls given to artists by the Serfoji kings of Tanjore.
Chandher dates the modern tradition to around Independence.
Kudanthai Chandher started puppetry.
Director Bharathiraja made a film called Bommalattam, using the puppet as a metaphor for cinema.
The twelve-string technique is nearly lost. Sahapedia says government support of Rs 2,000 per show barely covers travel.

future: Record the twelve-string technique with Sankaranathan, Murugan and others while it can still be shown, with video and written notes.
Pay for apprentices from puppeteer families and outside them.
Support a workshop where puppets can be made, with temple sculptors paid fairly, or lighter materials tested with the artists.
Raise the fee per show to cover transport, and plan festival tours.
Keep both the old mythological stories and new topical plays, as Chandher does.

name: Braj Raslila
tagline: Krishna's dance with Radha and the gopis, played by young boys in the lanes of Mathura and Vrindavan.
facts: Form: devotional dance-drama of the Krishna story
Home: Mathura and Vrindavan in the Braj region
Performers: young boys, trained in troupes called raas mandalis
Origin story: sources give different accounts and dates
art: Raslila is the dance-drama of Krishna's night dance with Radha and the gopis of Braj. The story is told in the Bhagavata Purana and the Gita Govinda. The name joins ras (nectar, feeling) and lila (play). In the story the gopis hear Krishna's flute, leave their homes and dance with him through the night.

In Braj the performance is a dance-drama of playful episodes from Krishna's life. Hinduism Today describes an opening ritual with arati, a conch and a temple bell, after which the guru and the audience bow to the lead performers. Performances are in temporary open-air pandals and are free to anyone who comes.

Hinduism Today says the shows run in August and September, in the monsoon, and that a season can last 45 days and nights. The same article says over 100 raas mandalis tour. A second search source said 30 to 40 troupes work in Braj today. The counts differ, so treat them as rough.
artist: Hinduism Today says all roles are played by male artists, and teenage boys play Radha. Boys join a troupe young, train long hours in dance, drama, music and school subjects, and follow a strict way of life that avoids meat, alcohol and smoking. Other writing says the main players are boys from brahmin families and that they are traditionally retired at puberty. I did not find a scholarly source for the second claim.

Devotional accounts treat the young performers as swarups, forms of the deities. The troupe is led by a teacher called a Rasacharya. I read only popular and devotional writing on this, not a scholarly study.
place: Braj is the land of Krishna's story, around Mathura and Vrindavan on the Yamuna in western Uttar Pradesh. Hinduism Today places Braj between Kosi and Agra.

Vrindavan is tied to the tradition by Wikipedia, which says performances there began at Vamshivata. Hinduism Today names Vishram Ghat in Mathura as the place of the first recorded raas leela. The two accounts differ.

history.what: Wikipedia says Swami Sri Uddhavaghamanda Devacharya of the Nimbarka tradition began the Vrindavan performances at Vamshivata.
Hinduism Today says the first recorded raas leela, based on the Bhagavata Purana, began at Vishram Ghat in Mathura under Vallabhacharya.
Wikipedia says Vallabhacharya and Vitthalanatha made the festival more prominent.

A journal article summarised in search results says Gaudiya followers name Narayanabhatta as the originator, and a popular belief links the idea to Vallabhacharya and Swami Haridas. Origins are not settled.
Raslila is staged each year in Mathura and Vrindavan, especially around Janmashtami and in the monsoon season.

future: Training: troupes train boys for years. Schooling alongside dance keeps the children's education secure.
Livelihood: touring and temple bookings pay for the troupes. Steady support for the Rasacharyas keeps the teaching alive.
Documentation: the SOAS Vrindavan Research Institute collection holds slides and records of Braj lilas, and more recordings would help.
Care of children: clear rules on welfare and schooling for young performers protect them.
Protection: Wikipedia lists no formal recognition for Braj Raslila. A heritage listing could be explored with the performers.

name: Burrakatha
tagline: A lead storyteller with a tambura and two answering voices, who turned a Shiva ballad into a voice for the people.
facts: Form: storytelling with song, dance and drums
Troupe: a lead performer and two co-performers
Grew from Jangam Katha, ballads about Shiva
Used in the 1940s to carry political messages
art: Burrakatha is a storytelling form of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The name comes from the burra, which one source says is the tambura worn on the performer's shoulder, and katha, meaning story.

The lead performer is the kathakudu. He plays the tambura, dances and tells the story. Wikipedia says he strikes two metal rings, called andelu, for rhythm. The two co-performers play clay drums called gummeta and respond with a chorus. They also interrupt with questions, jokes and comments on current affairs.
Wikipedia describes the mix as prayers, solo drama, dance, songs, poems and jokes. Stories may be from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, moral tales, or social and political issues of the day.
artist: Performers are village storytellers, and troupes are small. The form began with wandering Jangam minstrels, devotees of Shiva, and the Wikipedia article says the original form had two performers, a storyteller and his wife.

Shaik Nazar, also written Sheikh Nazer, is called the father of modern Burrakatha in the sources I read, for using it on contemporary issues. This title is repeated in Wikipedia and The Better India but I did not find an official citation for it.
I did not verify any awards for individual performers.
place: Burrakatha belongs to villages of the Telugu-speaking region. Wikipedia says the modern form was developed in Guntur around 1942 to spread political ideas among people who could not read, and that it became popular during the Telangana Rebellion.
It is also performed at festivals such as Dussehra and Sankranti, and on radio and television in Andhra Pradesh.

history.what: The form grew out of Jangam Katha, devotional songs of wandering Shiva minstrels. Over time secular material was added.

Activists used Burrakatha to speak against feudal landlords and colonial rule. The Better India reports that both the Madras government and the Nizam's government banned it. The Indian People's Theatre Association and the Praja Natya Mandali also used it.
The Better India notes an All India Radio broadcast of Burrakatha on the life of Netaji.
Television and later the internet drew audiences away, according to The Better India.
Governments have used it for public awareness on health, electricity and child marriage. Performers earn little, and for most it is no longer the main income.

future: Pay troupes for regular school and village shows, not only for government campaigns.
Record old Jangam Katha and Burrakatha performances, with the names of the artists.
Train younger performers and make sure they can earn a living from it.
Collect the histories of political Burrakatha from the 1940s while elderly witnesses are alive.
Offer new stories on local issues such as water, health and farming, so the form stays useful as well as old.

pins.label: Guntur, where the modern form grew

name: Chavittunatakam
tagline: Stamping-step opera of Kerala's coastal Latin Catholics, with crowned kings and emperors.
facts: Name means 'stamping drama'
Linked to the Latin Catholic coastal community
Dated to the 16th or 17th century; sources differ
Karlman (Charlemagne) is the most popular play
art: Chavittunatakam is a dance-drama of Kerala's Latin Catholics. Kerala Tourism says it blends music, dance, acting, dialogue and rhythm. Performers sing as they enter, followed by a chorus. Their stamping steps are called chuvadu. They also move face and eyes in time with the music.

Characters were mostly European kings and warriors, so costumes were colourful, with crowns, sceptres and shields. Kerala Tourism says they resembled Greek and Roman dress. A stage is built from wooden planks.
Sahapedia says the text is in an early form of Malayalam mixed with Senthamil and pidgin Latin. Kerala Tourism names two percussion instruments, the pada thamber and maravaladi.
Kerala Tourism lists early plays such as Brazeena, Ouseph, Kathrina and Karlman. Karlman is described as the most popular and still staged.
artist: Sahapedia says the art is performed by and for Latin Catholics, mainly fisher communities along the coast. It says the drama was developed by Portuguese missionaries to teach religious customs to new converts. Other accounts disagree, so the origin is contested.

Kerala Tourism names Chinna Thambi Annavi, a native of Tamil Nadu who came to Mattancherry, as the writer of the first play. It also names Vedanayakam Pillai of Neyyoor and others such as Anthony Annavi. Both early plays were in Tamil.
Sahapedia mentions Master A. N. Aniruddhan, whose disciples performed in a school festival video.
place: Plays were mostly staged on seashores where the Latin community lived. Kerala Tourism names Mattancherry, Gothuruth, Paravur, Ponjikkara, Kochi, Vallarpadom and Alappuzha. Gothuruth hosted a five-day chuvadu festival in the Muziris Heritage Area as part of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale.
Krupasanam, a study centre that encourages the art, is at Kalavoor, per Kerala Tourism.

history.what: Sahapedia dates the form to the 16th century.
Kerala Tourism dates it to the 17th century. Sources differ.
Annavi writes the first play, per Kerala Tourism.
Sahapedia says it has moved from religious use into theatre, storytelling and school festivals.
A chuvadu festival is held at Gothuruth as part of the Biennale.

future: Pay veteran troupes to teach the steps and singing to new generations.
Keep the old Tamil-Malayalam scripts safe by copying and publishing them.
Support school and college festivals, which already carry the form.
Help troupes with costumes, stage and travel costs.
Record full plays on video, with the stamping steps explained.

name: Dashavatara
tagline: Night-long Konkan plays on the ten forms of Vishnu, played by farmers and fishers.
facts: Form: folk theatre of South Konkan and North Goa
Tells of the ten avatars of Vishnu, with stories from the Ramayana and Mahabharata
Performed by men, who also play female roles
Touring season from October to May, per PARI
art: Dashavatara is a ritual-mythological theatre of the South Konkan, including Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg, and North Goa. A 2026 article in Critical Stages says it enacts the ten incarnations of Vishnu, with stories drawn mainly from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

The show has two parts. The purvaranga, or aad-dashavatar, is a devotional opening. The uttar-ranga, or akhyan, is the story itself, with dance and music. Critical Stages names the harmonium, mridangam and manjira as the main instruments.

Wooden masks were once central and were kept in a sacred box. The article says their use declined from the late 1980s because they are heavy, and make-up and headgear took their place. PARI says the plays are largely improvised, and the language changes with the venue: Sanskritised Marathi in temples, the local Malvani at homes.
artist: PARI reports that only men perform, mostly seasonal farmers and labourers. A company has about 15 members: 8 to 10 actors, three musicians and two cooks. Critical Stages says the Devali community, tied to temple service, historically played a key role in female roles.

PARI quotes the veteran actor Omprakash Chavan on how hard it is to live as a man who plays women's parts in a conservative society. Earnings are modest, and actors spend about Rs 300 per show on costume and make-up on average. It names the Yakshini Dashavatar Company and the Parcekar company as touring in the area.
Our approach: name the companies and actors, and show a night from the first drum beat to dawn.
place: PARI places the tradition in southern Maharashtra and northern Goa, with Sindhudurg district as the heartland. Companies tour villages from October, after the paddy harvest, until May, usually on contract from temples for the annual jatra for the village deity.

Shows start after midnight and end around 6 a.m. The audience includes local families and people who work in Mumbai and come home for the fair. PARI says the form is at least 500 years old, but we found no source for an exact origin or founder, and accounts of one differ.

history.what: The form is described as long established in the Konkan. Critical Stages gives no origin date.
Plays were staged in temple courtyards during jatras and ran through the night, according to Critical Stages.
Village shows were unamplified.
Microphones and loudspeakers arrive, and wooden masks decline, per Critical Stages.
Compressed formats become common, and the opening aad-dashavatar is often left out.
PARI follows companies on tour in Sindhudurg.

future: Training: young actors and musicians placed with senior companies.
Livelihood: better and steadier fees from temple committees and cultural bodies.
Materials: support for costumes, and for carving and keeping the old wooden masks.
Documentation: record the plays and the opening ritual before more of it is dropped.
Protection: respect for male actors in female roles, and funding for small companies.

name: Dastangoi
tagline: One voice, no props, and a tale of kings, tricksters and magic told in Urdu.
facts: Form: Urdu oral storytelling by one or two narrators
Best-known tale: the Dastan-e-Amir Hamza
Last traditional master: Mir Baqar Ali, died in Delhi in 1928
Revived in Delhi in 2005
art: Dastangoi comes from the Persian dastan (a tale) and goi (telling). A dastango tells long stories aloud. According to the Wikipedia article, the voice is the main tool. The teller needed some skill in drama, mime and even knowledge of warfare and politics.

The most famous cycle is the Dastan-e-Amir Hamza, the adventures of the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, which grew into a tale of war, magic and trickery. Wikipedia says Persian dastangos concentrated on Amir Hamza from the 14th century, and that the emperor Akbar commissioned the illustrated Hamzanama. Writer Abdul Halim Sharar grouped the themes of dastans as war, pleasure, beauty, love and deception.

In its modern form, as described by a 30 Stades profile, two narrators alternate. A show runs about 90 minutes and uses no music, visuals or props. Wikipedia notes that the singer and performer Syed Sahil Agha added music and singing from 2010.
Sources differ on the age of the art. Wikipedia gives the 13th century for the Urdu oral form and the 16th century for the Persian dastan style. Treat these dates as uncertain.
artist: Mir Baqar Ali is described as the last famous dastango of India. Wikipedia says he knew a vast number of verses by heart. After his death in 1928 the art went into a long silence.

Mahmood Farooqui, a writer, director and historian, started the revival. The 30 Stades profile says he met the Dastan-e-Amir Hamza around 2002, and in May 2005 staged the first modern show, based on Tilism-e-Hoshruba, with Himanshu Tyagi. Wikipedia also names Ankit Chadha, whose dastans were gathered in a 2019 book.

Farooqui has composed new dastans on subjects such as Partition, Bhagat Singh and the Mahabharata. The same profile says he has trained around 50 performers, including women, who were traditionally not part of the art, and that for some of them dastangoi is now a livelihood.
place: Dastangoi is an old storytelling art that came to Delhi through the Persian and Urdu world. Historian Ghaus Ansari, quoted on Wikipedia, traces its roots to pre-Islamic Arabia, from where it travelled through Iran to Delhi. Dastans were told in royal courts and in public places such as markets. Delhi was the city where the last great dastango, Mir Baqar Ali, died in 1928.

After the uprising of 1857, Wikipedia says several dastangos, writers and artists left Delhi for Lucknow. There the art was popular across classes and was heard in chowks, households and opium houses. So the story of the art runs between the two cities.

The modern revival also began in Delhi. In May 2005 the historian Mahmood Farooqui gave the first modern performance at the India International Centre. Today shows are held in theatres, schools, colleges and with NGOs. Venues change from year to year, so please check current listings.

history.what: Wikipedia dates the Urdu oral form to the 13th century and the Persian dastan style to the 16th. Sources differ.
Persian storytellers centre on the tale of Amir Hamza, per Wikipedia.
The emperor Akbar commissions the illustrated Hamzanama, a sister project to the oral tradition.
After the uprising, several dastangos and writers move from Delhi to Lucknow.
Nawal Kishore commissions a printed Hamza dastan, completed over about 25 years in 46 volumes.
Cinema, British rule and changing literary taste draw audiences away. Dastans come to be judged immoral by some.
Mir Baqar Ali, the last traditional dastango, dies in Delhi.
Mahmood Farooqui stages the first modern performance at the India International Centre, Delhi.
Syed Sahil Agha combines dastangoi with music and song; new storytellers join.

future: Training: keep the apprentice model that Farooqui describes, where new narrators learn the language, memory and timing from working tellers.
Livelihood: ticketed shows and school, college and NGO events already give some performers an income. More regular venues would help.
Material: the old dastans are in print, so new tellers can draw on the originals as well as on modern stories.
Documentation: record full performances with the text, so that listeners can compare the old and new styles.
Language: Urdu listening skills are the base of the art, so Urdu teaching in schools and clubs will decide how wide the audience can grow.

name: Garhwali Pandav Nritya
tagline: Villagers in Garhwal dance the Mahabharata for days, and sometimes become the heroes they play.
facts: Also called Pandav Lila
Performed outdoors, from three days to a month
Played by village amateurs, with dhol, damau and long bhankora trumpets
Best studied in William Sax's book Dancing the Self (2002)
art: Pandav Nritya, or Pandav Lila, is a ritual re-enactment of scenes from the Mahabharata through singing, dancing and recitation. It is practised in Garhwal, Uttarakhand.

The performance is outdoors and can last from three days to a month, depending on the village. It begins at night and runs into the early morning. As the action grows, it starts earlier in the day and goes through to the next morning.

The episodes are not told in order. The full epic is too long, so each group picks scenes the village knows well. The most awaited is the fight between Arjuna and his son, called gainda, after the rhinoceros that Arjuna kills.
The music is the dhol, the damau, and two long trumpets called bhankora. Weapons used in the play are worshipped and kept off the ground until the next performance.
artist: The performers are village amateurs, not professionals. They play the five Pandavas and other roles. Wikipedia says the performance is usually sponsored by the Janman, a Kshatriya group.
Sax and others report that performers sometimes become possessed by the spirits of the characters and begin to dance. This is described as part of the ritual, not an act.
The sources I read do not name individual performers.
place: Pandav Lila is found across Garhwal. Sax has written that in any year most villagers in Garhwal are probably within walking distance of a performance.
Each village can have its own version, with some stressing song and others drama. The sources I read do not give a season or list specific villages, so none are named here.

history.what: Wikipedia says the origins are interwoven with Hindu mythology and gives no firm dates or documents. I found no earlier source.
William Sax published a paper on the Arjuna and rhinoceros episode in the Journal of the American Oriental Society.
Sax's book Dancing the Self: Personhood and Performance in the Pandav Lila of Garhwal appeared from Oxford University Press, based on about ten years of study.
Andrew Alter wrote on the form in Ethnomusicology Forum.

future: Training: let young villagers take roles and learn the songs and drum patterns.
Livelihood: support the drummers and singers who keep the performance going.
Materials: keep the ritual weapons, costumes and instruments made and repaired locally.
Documentation: record performances in each village with the people who sing and dance them.
Protection: keep it a village ritual, with the community deciding how it is shown to outsiders.

name: Harikatha
tagline: One storyteller on his feet for hours, singing, speaking and acting out a saint's life.
facts: Also called Harikatha Kalakshepam, and kirtan in Marathi
One main performer stands throughout, with a violin, mridangam and tambura behind
Tanjore Krishna Bhagavatar (1841-1903) is credited with giving it its modern shape
Strongest in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra and Karnataka
art: Harikatha is a storytelling art in which one performer, the Haridasa or bhagavatar, narrates a saint's life or an episode from the epics. Wikipedia calls it a composite art of storytelling, poetry, music, drama, dance and philosophy. The aim is devotion and moral teaching.

A Tamil Nadu performance, as described by the scholar Sriram V., has three parts: an invocation (panchapadi), a first section (prathamapadi) and the main story (nirupanam). The performer stands throughout and keeps time with a pair of small cymbals called chipla. He wears ankle bells. Behind him sit a violinist or harmonium player, a mridangam player, a tambura player who holds the pitch, and sometimes a cymbal player.

The performer mixes stories with songs, jokes and short asides. Songs are in the language of the audience and in Sanskrit. In the Telugu tradition, performers called haridasus also walk through villages singing in the month before Sankranti, according to Wikipedia.
artist: Sriram V. writes that Tanjore Krishna Bhagavatar (1841-1903) studied both the northern (Marathi) and southern katha traditions and combined them, and that he fixed how the performer and accompanists sit and wrote popular nirupanams such as Rukmini Kalyanam. Later exponents named include Harikesanallur Muthiah Bhagavatar, Mangudi Chidambara Bhagavatar and Kallidaikurichi Vedanta Bhagavatar.

Women entered the art in the 20th century. C. Saraswathi Bai is usually cited as the first woman performer, in 1907, though other claims exist and Sriram V. notes the dispute. Padmasini Bai and C. Banni Bai are also named. Wikipedia says Saraswathi Bai broke the male Brahmin monopoly on the art.

In Andhra, Ajjada Adibhatla Narayana Dasu is credited with starting the Telugu form after seeing a performance in Madras in 1883, and with founding a school in Vizianagaram. In Karnataka, Wikipedia names Purandara Dasa and Kanaka Dasa as famous Haridasas of the bhakti tradition.
place: Harikatha is a southern form with a Maharashtrian root. In Maharashtra it is kirtan, tied to the Warkari poet-saints and the town of Pandharpur. Sriram V. explains that kirtankars from Maharashtra came to the Maratha court of Thanjavur, where Sarabhoji II supported the arts, and their style met the Tamil katha tradition there.

From Thanjavur the form spread across Tamil Nadu. In Andhra it centres on the coast and Vizianagaram. Kerala has its own related strands, including kathaprasangam. In Karnataka it is linked to the Dasa tradition. Our pins mark Pandharpur, Thanjavur, Vizianagaram and Thiruvananthapuram.

history.what: Dasa saints in Karnataka tell and sing of Hari. Wikipedia places the present form of Harikatha in the bhakti movement; sources differ on dates.
Katha kalakshepam in the south is a scholarly discourse based on texts like the Periya Puranam, according to Sriram V.
Sarabhoji II of Thanjavur supports arts, and Marathi kirtankars gain favour at court.
Tanjore Krishna Bhagavatar blends the northern and southern styles.
Ajjada Adibhatla Narayana Dasu sees a Harikatha performance in Madras, then begins the Telugu form.
C. Saraswathi Bai is usually cited as the first woman performer.
TR Kamala Murthy, who kept the traditional form, receives the Kalaimamani title.

future: Offer apprenticeships in which young performers learn nirupanams, staging and accompaniment from senior bhagavatars.
Record full-length performances with notes in the local language, in an open archive.
Support women and performers from all communities, building on the path Saraswathi Bai opened.
Pay accompanists such as violinists and mridangam players fairly for festival and temple programmes.
Bring Harikatha into schools and radio in short, lively forms, so the stories reach younger listeners.

name: Jat-Jatin
tagline: A song-and-dance drama of a couple apart, and a call for rain.
facts: Region: Mithila and Kosi, north Bihar, and across the border in Nepal
Often described as a couple's dance, sometimes as a rain ritual
Accompanied by dholak and manjira, per Wikipedia
Sources disagree on who performs it and on what it is
art: Jat-Jatin is a folk performance of Mithila. Sources describe it in different ways. Wikipedia and a Bihar folk-dance guide call it a dance for a man and a woman, usually in the monsoon. It shows the lovers Jat and Jatin and their separation, as the man prepares to leave for work and the woman grieves.

A different account says it is performed by women during drought, to ask Indra for rain. Wikipedia gives this under tradition, and a Maithili academic thesis quoted in a search summary calls it a dramatic ritual rather than a drama with a plot. We could not open that thesis, so this is not confirmed.
Music is simple: dholak and manjira, and group singing. The guide says its themes later grew to include drought, floods, poverty and family life.
artist: We found no reliable source naming individual performers or troupes of Jat-Jatin. The sources describe the form but not the people who keep it alive.
That is itself a finding. Jat-Jatin appears mostly in general folk-dance lists, and little documentation by researchers was found.
place: Jat-Jatin belongs to Mithila, which spans north Bihar and southern Nepal. Sources place it especially in the Mithila and Kosi regions.
The Kosi plain floods in some years and goes without rain in others, which fits the stories of flood, drought and separation the songs are said to carry.

history.what: Wikipedia calls it an ancient Mithila practice. No dated source was found.
Separation of the lovers Jat and Jatin, per a Bihar folk-dance guide.
Drought, floods, poverty and social struggles were added, per the same guide.
Sources are mostly general lists. A thorough record by scholars or the Akademi was not found.

future: Training: find and support the families who still perform
Livelihood: pay for performances at fairs and festivals
Materials: keep the dholak and manjira song tradition with the performers
Documentation: record songs, story and rain rituals before they fade, and settle the question of dance or drama with the performers themselves
Protection: look for state or national recognition once fieldwork exists

name: Jatra
tagline: Bengal's open-air folk theatre of song, drama and a roaring crowd.
facts: Folk theatre combining acting, song, music and dance
Earliest described performance in Brindavan Das's Chaitanyabhagavad (1548)
Chitpur Road in Kolkata was the old jatra district
Phanibhusan Bidyabinod: first jatra artist to win a Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1968)
art: Jatra is a folk drama of Bengal and nearby regions. Banglapedia says a performance has acting, song, music and dance, and was usually staged on a temporary raised platform with the audience seated around it.

A typical show lasted about four hours and ran in five acts with songs, dances and comic interludes. The adhikari, a manager and narrator, played a central role. A troupe usually had 50 to 60 members.
The old Krishna Jatra stressed love and had no women actors. Later forms took in Shakti and Nath stories, Vidyasundar, and nationalist and social plays.
artist: Banglapedia names Mukunda Das, whose Swadeshi Jatra Party brought patriotic themes after World War I. Wikipedia names Phanibhusan Bidyabinod, the first jatra artist to receive the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, in 1968.
Theatre directors Utpal Dutt and Sombhu Mitra drew on jatra's style, says Wikipedia.
Most companies today are business-owned, and Wikipedia says their style often reflects films and TV serials.
place: Jatra belongs to rural Bengal, Odisha, Assam, Tripura and Bangladesh. In Kolkata, Chitpur Road was the jatra district; Wikipedia counts about 55 troupes based there in 2005.

The same page reports that in 2005 jatra was performed on nearly 4,000 stages in West Bengal, and in 2001 more than 300 companies employed over 20,000 people. These are reported figures, not recent ones.

history.what: Wikipedia says Chaitanya reportedly played Rukmini in 1507; Banglapedia gives Brindavan Das's account of 1548. Sources differ.
Krishna Jatra dominant.
Shakti, Nath and Pala forms; Vidyasundar marks a turn to secular themes.
Natun Jatra adds dance, prose dialogue and secular themes.
Swadeshi jatra turns to protest; the British ban some plays.
First Kolkata jatra festival, part of a revival.
Phanibhusan Bidyabinod wins the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award.

future: Training: schools for actors, singers and musicians outside the big companies.
Livelihood: fair pay for troupe members and steady bookings.
Materials: keep live music and local language.
Documentation: archive scripts and old recordings.
Protection: support rural troupes against the pull of film and TV.

name: Kathputli
tagline: Wooden string puppets in long skirts, and a hidden puppeteer whose voice is a whistle.
facts: Form: string puppetry (marionette theatre)
Community: the Bhat, also called Nat, puppeteers
Puppet: about 30 cm tall, carved head, usually no legs
Age: said to be a thousand years or more, but not firmly documented
art: Kathputli comes from kath (wood) and putli (doll). It is the string puppet theatre of Rajasthan. The Wikipedia article calls it the most popular form of Indian puppetry. A string runs from the top of each puppet to the puppeteer above.

The Incredible India page says each puppet is carved from a single piece of wood, including its headgear, and stands about 30 cm tall. The eyes are long and stylised and the face is usually painted yellow. The body and limbs are made of mango wood and stuffed with cotton. Most puppets have no legs. A long trailing skirt hides this, and the figure moves freely.

The stage is simple. Two string beds are stood upright with bamboo poles tied across, a dark curtain hangs at the back, and a coloured three-arched curtain called tibara hangs in front to hide the puppeteers. The puppeteers control the hands, neck and shoulders through strings wound around their fingers. A dholak gives the rhythm and women sing songs that go with the dialogue.

The puppets do not speak in an ordinary voice. Sources describe a small instrument called the boli, held in the puppeteer's mouth, that makes a high, whistle-like sound. One source says a narrator outside the stage tells the audience what the whistles mean. Sources differ on how to describe the boli: some say a bamboo whistle, others a pair of bamboo sticks with a stretched strip of tape. Nazir Ali Jairazbhoy's book Kathputli: The World of Rajasthani Puppeteers is cited as describing it in detail.

The best-known story is about Amar Singh Rathore, a warrior said to have lived in the time of Shah Jahan. Many shows today also carry messages about dowry, literacy, health and cleanliness, according to the Incredible India page.
artist: The art is practised mainly by the Bhat community, also called Nat. They were a travelling people who went from village to village with a portable theatre. Sources place them especially in Nagaur, Churu and Sikar districts. Sources say they perform in the dry season and return to farm after the rains. Many have since settled in different parts of Rajasthan.

The Bhats say their ancestors performed for royal families and were honoured by Rajasthan's rulers. Wikipedia says kings and rich families supported the artists for about 500 years, and that in return the artists sang the praises of the patrons' ancestors. A University of Toronto exhibit is more cautious. It says there are signs the tradition existed in Mughal times, but that many Bhat families took up puppetry only within the last hundred years or so. Dates are not settled.

Two names appear in the sources as Sangeet Natak Akademi awardees: Puran Bhat and Naurang Bhat. One source says Puran Bhat founded the Aakar Puppet Theatre in the 1980s, which brought kathputli into themed, social shows. I did not check the award years.

Several families have settled in Kathputli Colony in Shadipur, Delhi. It began in the 1950s as tents of travelling performers from Rajasthan. It now holds puppeteers as well as magicians, acrobats, musicians and others. Not every resident is a Bhat puppeteer.
place: Kathputli belongs to the dry land of Rajasthan, in the Thar region. Scholars think it may have begun around Nagaur and nearby areas. Mango wood, cotton cloth, bamboo and bright cloth scraps are the main materials. Sources I read do not say where the mango wood is bought.

Two institutions in Rajasthan work with the art. Bharatiya Lok Kala Mandal in Udaipur was founded in 1952 by Devilal Samar and runs a puppet theatre and museum. Rupayan Sansthan in Jodhpur was founded in 1960 by Vijaydan Detha and Komal Kothari and documents folk arts. Jaipur and Jaisalmer are the main places where visitors see shows and buy puppets as souvenirs.

Kathputli Colony in Shadipur, West Delhi, was chosen by the Delhi Development Authority in 2007 for the city's first in-situ slum rehabilitation project. A private builder, Raheja Developers, signed a contract in 2009. Residents were to be moved to a transit camp in Anand Parbat while new flats were built. Residents protested and went to court, and counts of households differed between the DDA and the builder. A 2018 report says a foundation stone was laid. A 2023 Land Conflict Watch update says the puppeteers were still waiting. Please check recent news for the present position.

history.what: Popular sources say a thousand to fifteen hundred years. Written records from before the colonial period are thin, and scholars do not agree on a date.
The Bhats say their ancestors performed before Rajasthan's rulers. Wikipedia describes around 500 years of royal and noble support.
The tale of Amar Singh Rathore, who is said to have lived around the time of Shah Jahan and is linked to Nagaur, becomes the best-known kathputli story.
Travelling performers from Rajasthan pitch tents in Shadipur, Delhi, the start of Kathputli Colony.
Bharatiya Lok Kala Mandal, Udaipur, is founded; it keeps a puppet museum.
Rupayan Sansthan, Jodhpur, is founded by Vijaydan Detha and Komal Kothari.
Nazir Ali Jairazbhoy does the fieldwork behind his book on Rajasthani puppeteers.
The DDA picks Kathputli Colony for in-situ redevelopment; a private partner signs in 2009.
Residents are moved towards the transit camp amid protest; a foundation stone is laid in 2018.
Land Conflict Watch reports that the puppeteers were still awaiting rehabilitation.

future: Keep the puppeteers' homes and workspace in any redevelopment, with a rehearsal and workshop hall built in, and involve the families in the plan.
Run apprenticeships so that children learn carving, costume and boli alongside school.
Document the repertoire, the songs and the boli technique on film with Bhat elders, and return copies to the families.
Pay puppet makers fairly for the carved figures sold as souvenirs, and name the family on each piece.
Bring shows to schools and villages through the year so that artists do not depend only on tourist seasons.
Check the status of the GI claim (one government page mentions a 2006 tag) and apply for protection if it has not been done properly.
