name: Koodiyattam
tagline: Sanskrit theatre played in temple halls, where one scene can last for days.
facts: Form: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala
UNESCO: proclaimed 2001, on the Representative List 2008
Performers: Chakyar men, Nangiar women, Nambiar drummers
Drum: the copper mizhavu
art: Koodiyattam (also spelled Kutiyattam) is a Sanskrit theatre tradition of Kerala. UNESCO describes it as one of India's oldest living theatre traditions, and says its origins go back more than 2,000 years. Scholars do not agree on an exact date.

It is an actor's theatre. Acting relies on eye expression (netra abhinaya) and gesture (hasta abhinaya). UNESCO notes that a single act can take days, and that a full performance can last up to 40 days.
The stage is a temple hall called a koothambalam or kuttampalam, with an oil lamp on stage as a sign of the divine presence. A great copper drum, the mizhavu, anchors the sound.
The Vidushaka, the clown, has a special place. Kerala Tourism says he speaks in the local language so that the audience can follow the story and he also makes satirical jokes.
The form is also a source for other arts. Kerala Tourism notes that Kathakali took gesture and expression technique from Koodiyattam.
artist: The hereditary performers are the Chakyar community, whose men play male roles, and the Nangiar (Nambiar) women who play female roles and also chant Sanskrit verse and play cymbals. Nambiar men play the mizhavu.
UNESCO says actors train for ten to fifteen years. Families held the acting manuals as closely guarded property until recent times.

In the 20th century the Chakyar master Mani Madhava Chakyar broke with custom by teaching non-Chakyars, including Nambiar students and foreigners, and by taking Koodiyattam out of temple precincts, according to Wikipedia. It also records the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1964 and the Padma Shri in 1974 for him. The Kerala tourism biography notes that Ammannur Madhava Chakyar received the UNESCO citation in 2001. These honours come from Wikipedia and a single tourism biography, and should be checked against official records before publication.
Kerala Kalamandalam now teaches Koodiyattam and Nangiar Koothu, and women and men from many backgrounds train in it.
Our approach: sit with the families who have kept the manuals, and let them speak for the art.
place: Koodiyattam belongs to central Kerala, the old Cochin kingdom, and to the temples that once paid for it. Kerala Tourism names the Koodalmanikyam Temple in Irinjalakuda and the Vadakkumnathan Temple in Thrissur as major performance sites.
Training centres include the Ammannur Gurukulam in Irinjalakuda, Kerala Kalamandalam at Cheruthuruthy, and the Margi centre in Thiruvananthapuram in the south.
The koothambalam is a hall inside the temple compound, so access for visitors depends on temple rules.

history.what: Scholars place the origins at around 2,000 years ago, a claim that UNESCO repeats. There is little firm evidence for early centuries.

Kulashekhara Varman of the Chera line is traditionally credited with reforming the practice and writing two performance texts. Kerala Tourism names him Kulashekhara Perumal; the exact date is debated by historians.
UNESCO notes that patronage collapsed with the feudal order, leaving the families in serious difficulty.
A revival began. Mani Madhava Chakyar took the art to wider audiences.
Mani Madhava Chakyar received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, according to Wikipedia.
UNESCO proclaimed Koodiyattam a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
It was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
UNESCO notes continuing funding problems for the families. Kalamandalam, Margi and Ammannur Gurukulam train new artists.

future: Give the hereditary families regular stipends for teaching, so performance does not rely on the temple calendar alone.
Record complete performances and the acting manuals, in agreement with the families who own them.
Offer scholarships for students from outside the Chakyar and Nambiar families, as the great masters did.
Make more temple halls and school halls available for regular shows, with short introductions in English and Malayalam.
Train a new generation of mizhavu makers and players, since the craft of the copper drum is small and fragile.
Create a documentation centre in Irinjalakuda, linked to the UNESCO listing, for scripts, photographs and film.

name: Lai Haraoba
tagline: The merry-making of the gods: a Meitei ritual that enacts creation in dance, song and procession.
facts: Held at shrines of the umanglai deities, roughly February to May-June
Lasts from about three days to over three weeks, by shrine
Led by maibas, maibis and the pena player
Source of Manipuri classical dance, say scholars
art: Lai Haraoba is a religious festival of the Meitei people, held at neighbourhood shrines of the umanglai deities. Scholars translate the name differently: Elangbam Nilakanta Singh gives merry-making of the gods and goddesses, and Parratt and Parratt give pleasing of the gods.

Sahapedia describes three stages. In Lai Eekouba the shrine doors, shut all year, are opened, and a procession goes to a pond or river where a maibi invokes the sacred presence. In the middle days, called Haraoba, the pena is played at dawn, and in the evening come flower offerings, the thougal jagoi dance and the laibou procession, which enacts creation, birth, house-building, cultivation, weaving and fishing. In Lairoi the sacred time and space are closed, with a blade dance, a comic skit and the sending back of the deity.

Dance is part of the ritual itself. Sahapedia says these ritual dances are the source of the Manipuri dance form and have inspired Manipuri Ras Lila. Singing is collective, in call and answer, led by the maiba.
artist: The festival is led by ritual specialists. Maibas are men and maibis are women who act as spirit mediums, lead dances and invocations, and carry out the central transfer of the sacred. The asheiba, the pena player, is a man; Sahapedia says the maiba and asheiba lineages are open only to men.
Beyond the specialists, the whole neighbourhood prepares for the festival, and people of all ages carry sacred items and make offerings.
Since dance entered the curriculum of the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy, Sahapedia notes, traditional dances have also entered institutionally trained repertoires and stage adaptations.
place: Each shrine sets its own dates and customs. Sahapedia lists four main kinds. Kanglei, around Imphal and Kangla, centres on Pakhangba. Moirang, in the south of the valley, centres on Thangjing and includes the Khamba-Thoibi duet. Chakpa, in villages such as Andro and Phayeng, has simpler hand movements. Kakching, east of Imphal, is known for the eel-hunting rite on the last day. Scholars count the types differently.
The festival is also held in Meitei settlements in Assam, Tripura, Bangladesh and Myanmar.

history.what: Folklore holds that the gods first held it on Koubru Hill; Wikipedia gives this as folklore. It is said to be observed since ancient times.
The rites honour the umanglai, more than 300 deities according to Sahapedia, and a presiding pair, Lainingthou and Lairembi.
Sahapedia says accounts linking Lai Haraoba to Hindu deities were once popular in some circles but are not readily accepted by most Meiteis today.
Sporting events such as kangjei and mukna, once held the day after Lairoi, are less emphasised now.
Wikipedia says it is not yet inscribed by UNESCO and that the Manipur government has sought recognition.

future: Training: support asheibas, maibas and maibis to teach younger people, since the roles pass through lineages.
Livelihood: keep shrine communities able to host the festival, including costumes, offerings and musicians.
Documentation: record each shrine's own rites and songs before they fade, with community consent.
Protection: keep the ritual meaning in view when it is shown on stage.
Recognition: any heritage listing should follow the wishes of the shrine communities.

name: Nangiar Koothu
tagline: A woman's solo temple theatre of Kerala, drawn from Koodiyattam and told through eyes and hands.
facts: Solo performance by a woman, derived from Koodiyattam
Koodiyattam: UNESCO Masterpiece proclaimed in 2001
Performed traditionally in temple koothambalams
Margi Sathi (1965 to 2015) was a leading exponent
art: Nangiar Koothu is a performing art derived from Koodiyattam, the Sanskrit theatre of Kerala. Wikipedia describes it as performed by women. A single woman acts out a story, usually through facial expression and hand gesture.
Koodiyattam was traditionally staged in temple theatres called koothambalams. Artists train from a young age in music, rhythm, dance, gesture, makeup and Sanskrit.
Margi Sathi wrote performance manuals for several Nangiar Koothu productions. Her manual for Sreeramacharitham, the Rama story told from Sita's view, was published in 1999, per Wikipedia.
artist: Sources differ on community. Wikipedia's Margi Sathi page says women of the Chakkyar community perform it. Its Koodiyattam page says women called Nangyaramma, of the Ambalavasi Nambiar caste, played the female roles, and that Chakyar women were not allowed to take part.

Margi Sathi (P. S. Sathi Devi) was born in Cheruthuruthy, trained at Kerala Kalamandalam and under Painkulam Rama Chakyar, and joined the Margi institute in 1988. She performed at UNESCO in Paris in 2001, and received the Kerala Sangeetha Nataka Akademi award in 2002. She died on 1 December 2015.
Ammannur Madhava Chakyar (1917 to 2008) took Koodiyattam abroad in the 1980s and received the UNESCO citation in 2001. His students named by The News Minute include Usha Nangiyar.
place: Koodiyattam is performed in select temples of Kerala. Cheruthuruthy in Thrissur district, home of Kerala Kalamandalam, is the base for many artists.
Ammannur Madhava Chakyar's family is associated with Irinjalakuda. I have not read a source that places Nangiar Koothu there specifically, so the pin is approximate.

history.what: The Chera ruler Kulasekhara Varma is believed to have reformed Koodiyattam, per Wikipedia.
Loss of feudal patronage hurts performers.
A revival begins.
Mani Madhava Chakyar performs in Chennai, the first time Koodiyattam is staged outside Kerala, per Wikipedia.
UNESCO proclaims Koodiyattam a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
Margi Sathi dies.

future: Train girls early and keep teachers paid, as the art needs years of practice.
Keep performance manuals (attaprakaram) such as Sathi's available to students.
Support performance outside temples while keeping temple performance alive.
Document the solo repertoire on video with senior artists.
Find steady income for women performers, since patronage is thin.

name: Nautanki
tagline: Night-long operatic theatre of the Hindi heartland, driven by the thunder of a pair of kettledrums.
facts: Form: sung folk opera with dialogue, dance and humour
Two main styles: Hathras and Kanpur
Took its name from the play Shehzadi Nautanki
Early script books sold in huge numbers; Shrikrishna Pustakalaya reportedly sold about 75 million copies until 1971
art: Nautanki is an operatic theatre of north India that joins music, dance, storytelling, dialogue, humour and pathos. Sahapedia says it emerged in the late nineteenth century in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, which is today's Uttar Pradesh. Its forerunners were bhagat, ballads sung by wandering bards, and improvised skits.

The form was first called svang. The name nautanki came after a hit play, Shehzadi Nautanki, a Punjabi folk tale that became very popular around Kanpur. Other explanations of the name are repeated in popular writing, but they are less well documented.

A pair of large kettledrums called nakkara gives nautanki its sound, and the beat was meant to carry for miles. The harmonium, clarinet and dholak are also used. Verse forms such as doha, chaubola and daur carry the story. A show begins with a prayer to Saraswati and Ganesha, and a sutradhar summarises the tale in song.

The two best-known styles take their names from towns. The Hathras style stays closer to svang and to classical singing, and opens with dhrupad in which singers hold long notes. The Kanpur style uses simpler music and puts more weight on dialogue and acting. Sources differ on how much Parsi theatre shaped the Kanpur style.

The repertoire draws on legend, Sanskrit drama, Persian romance and myth. Plays such as Raja Harishchandra, Laila Majnu, Shirin Farhad and Heer Ranjha are popular. Some plays carry social messages, and during the freedom movement troupes staged patriotic pieces.
artist: Sahapedia names Indarman, a poet of the Chhipi caste, as the man who began staging svangs in Hathras in the 1890s. His most accomplished disciple, Natharam Gaur, was a singer, dancer, composer and actor who often played women's roles. He also founded the Shyam Press in Hathras, which printed script books.

Early troupes were all male. From the 1930s women joined, more so in Kanpur than in Hathras. Gulab Bai set up the Great Gulab Theatre Company and, according to Sahapedia, received the Sangeet Natak Akademi award in 1985 and the Padma Shri in 1990. Shrikrishna Pehelwan of Kanpur, who ran the Shrikrishna Pustakalaya, received the Sangeet Natak Akademi award in 1968.

Script books were a big part of the story. Shrikrishna Pustakalaya reportedly sold about 75 million copies up to 1971, and more than 400 titles were published. The press still operates today, says Sahapedia.
place: Nautanki belongs to the plains of western and central Uttar Pradesh. Hathras, in the west, and Kanpur, on the Ganga in the centre, became its two main hubs. Kanpur rose as a centre by the 1910s.

Plays were staged in the open on temporary stages, often from late night until dawn, and could draw a whole village. From the 1930s Parsi theatre led some companies to use proscenium stages, painted backdrops and richer costume.
Today Sahapedia says working troupes survive in places such as Hathras, Mathura, Unnao and Beeghapur.

history.what: Indarman begins staging svangs in Hathras; Natharam Gaur becomes his leading disciple.
A play called Shehzadi Nautanki becomes a hit, and the form takes its name from it.
Kanpur emerges as a second major centre with its own style.
Plays on the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and on civil disobedience are staged, according to Sahapedia.
Women begin to join troupes; ticket sales support professionally managed companies.
Police stop Trimohan Lal's Kanpur show Aurat ka Pyar; the city bans his company until 1947.
The flow reverses: nautanki adapts popular films, where early cinema had borrowed from it.
Most companies collapse for lack of capital and competition from cinema and television.

future: Training: Sahapedia notes there is no formal training system for young performers, so a school or guru-based course is the first need.
Livelihood: invitations from bodies such as the Hindi Akademi in Delhi and the Sangeet Natak Akademi in Lucknow have grown. Paid, regular bookings would help troupes stay together.
Documentation: more than 400 published script books exist. Scanning and cataloguing them would protect the repertoire.
Audiences: new plays by dramatists who adapt nautanki, and recordings online, can reach younger viewers.
Protection: support for the older troupes, such as the Great Gulab Theatre Company and Krishna Kala Kendra, keeps living knowledge of both styles.

name: Oggu Katha
tagline: Sung stories of Mallanna and Yellamma, opened with the beat of a small damaru.
facts: Form: sung and acted ballad
Subjects: Mallanna, Beerappa, Yellamma
Communities: Golla (Yadava) and Kuruma (Kuruba)
Instruments: damarukam (jaggu), dolu, brass talas
art: Oggu Katha is a form of sung storytelling from Telangana. A team of four to six performers tells the stories of Mallanna (Mallikarjuna), Beerappa and Yellamma. Wikipedia says the verse form is manjari dwipada.

The main narrator and a helper switch between characters, which gives the telling a dramatic quality. The damarukam, called jaggu, opens each story. Other instruments include the dolu, the large rana bheri drum, brass talas, the kanjira and a wind instrument, the napheera.

Feminism in India reports that performers also speak the nine emotions (nava rasa) and that the art is performed at festivals, weddings and other occasions. Oggu Katha is closely tied to pilgrimage and festival times.
artist: Wikipedia describes the Oggus as traditional priests of the Golla Kurumas. The art began among the Golla (Yadava) and Kuruma (Kuruba) communities.

Feminism in India profiles Jamma Mallari of Medipally village, described as the only woman Oggu Katha artist. She learned from her father from the age of 11 and won a Woman Achiever Award in 2020. Men have traditionally played the female roles. The article says she is no longer able to perform at 80.
Wikipedia lists notable performers including Chukka Sattaiah, Kathala Mallaiah, Midde Ramulu and Bala Siddulu, but notes the page needs more citations.
place: Komuravelli in Siddipet district has the Mallanna temple on a hill. Devotees gather there at Maha Shivaratri and during the Jatara season. Wikipedia places Komuravelli in Warangal district, which is an older description.
The tradition is carried across Telangana by touring teams, mostly in villages.

history.what: No source I read gives a firm date for when Oggu Katha began.
Wikipedia ties the name to the oggu, the folk name for Shiva's damaru, which opens each story. Other explanations exist and I could not confirm the origin from a scholarly source.
A report cited by Wikipedia says the Telangana government has promoted the tradition.
Jamma Mallari receives a Woman Achiever Award as a folk artist.
A University of Hyderabad workshop brings Komuravelli performers together with students for documentation (reported on its news site).

future: Training: formal classes in schools and colleges, as the Feminism in India article suggests, and openings for women.
Livelihood: paid festival and stage performances through the year.
Materials: support for makers of the dolu, rana bheri and damaru.
Documentation: record the Mallanna story, which has no written script, with the performers.
Protection: keep the tradition with the Golla and Kuruma families who carry it, with their consent for any recordings.

name: Ojapali
tagline: One lead singer, a chorus and a pair of cymbals tell the old stories.
facts: An oja leads, a chorus of pali answers
Main instrument: khutitaal (small cymbals)
Forms include Byah, Sukananni, Ramayani and Sattriya
Historically centred in Darrang
art: Ojapali is a narrative song-dance tradition of Assam. A lead performer, the oja, and a chorus, the pali, tell a story together. Wikipedia says a troupe usually has one oja and four or five pali. The chief chorister, the daina-pali, stands to the oja's right and moves the story on with questions and explanation.
The performance mixes sung verses, dialogue, rhythmic footwork, gesture and semi-improvised acting. The main instrument is the khutitaal, small cymbals.

There are several kinds. Byah (also called Bigoya) tells epic stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana. Sukananni, also called Maroi-gowa, is centred on the serpent goddess Manasa and the Beula-Lakhindar story. Ramayani sticks to Ramayana episodes. Sattriya Ojapali grew in the sattra setting. Sources spell Sukananni in several ways, including Suknani.
Wikipedia notes that beyond ritual, Ojapali has taught morals, kept community memory alive and, in the twentieth century, helped bring people together for public causes.
artist: Performers are often village artists who learn from a senior oja. The Assam Tribune says the form has been kept alive mainly by dedicated artistes, many of them with little formal schooling.

Wikipedia names Lalit Chandra Nath, a Sukananni exponent, who received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1983 and the Akademi's Tagore Award in 2012. Kinaram Nath Oja received the Akademi Award in 2012 for Sukanani Ojapali. It also names Durgabar Kayastha as an early poet-performer linked to Durgavari Ojapali.
Troupes have found livelihood hard, especially during the Covid-19 pandemic, as Wikipedia notes.
place: The tradition is historically centred on Darrang, around Mangaldai and Sipajhar. It continues in Nalbari, Kamrup, Bajali, Baksa and Udalguri, and practitioners are active near Tezpur.
At a talk in Darrang reported by the Assam Tribune, speakers pointed to its appeal to rural people across caste, creed and religion.

history.what: Scholars date its development well before the neo-Vaishnavite movement; it is rooted in the wider Indian kathakata tradition of epic storytelling.
Wikipedia says Ojapali was patronised in Darrang under King Dharmanarayana.
It meets the Bhakti movement. Some scholars suggest it influenced Sankardeva's theatre (Ankiya Nat and Bhaona); this is a scholarly suggestion, not settled.
Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards go to Lalit Chandra Nath (1983) and Kinaram Nath Oja (2012).

future: Training: add Ojapali to school and college events and, as Dr Kanak Chandra Saharia proposed, to university study at Gauhati University.
Livelihood: steady invitations, pensions and fair fees for troupes outside festival season.
Documentation: record each form, Byah, Sukananni and Ramayani, with full texts and tunes from living ojas.
Materials: khutitaal makers and cymbal supply should be traced and supported.
Protection: support for senior exponents, some of whom do not get an artist's pension according to news reports.

name: Ottamthullal
tagline: A solo dance-recital in green makeup that wraps sharp social satire in Puranic stories.
facts: Form: solo recitation with dance, in Malayalam
Traditionally credited to Kunchan Nambiar (1705 to 1770)
Accompanied by mridangam or idakka, and ilathalam
Performer wears green makeup and bright costume
art: Ottamthullal is a recite-and-dance form. One performer acts and dances while reciting verse. A chorus or other artists repeat each finished sentence. The music uses a mridangam or idakka and a pair of ilathalam cymbals.

The solo performer wears green makeup and a colourful costume with a long red and white band and painted wooden ornaments, per Wikipedia. The language is plain, everyday Malayalam, with old sayings and folk wisdom.
The themes come from the Puranas and epics, but the telling is full of humour and social comment. Kunchan Nambiar's stories include Syamanthakam, Ghoshayathra, Kiratham and Bakavadham.
artist: Kunchan Nambiar was born on 5 May 1705 at Kalakkathu Veedu in Killikkurussimangalam, Palakkad district, according to Wikipedia. He later lived in Ambalappuzha and served the court of Marthanda Varma of Travancore from 1748. He died in 1770. Kerala observes 5 May as Kunchan Day.

A popular story says Nambiar fell asleep while playing the mizhavu for a Chakyar Koothu, was mocked by the Chakyar, and created Ottamthullal in reply. Sources present this as a legend, not documented fact.
Counts of his works vary. One source says 64 thullal stories, another lists about 41. His verse is known for social criticism wrapped in humour.
Wikipedia names Mathur Panikkar as a performer who helped bring the form to modern audiences, but the claim is not cited.
place: Killikkurussimangalam, Nambiar's birthplace, is in Palakkad district. The Kunchan Nambiar Memorial Society runs memorials, including the Kunchan Smarakam in Palakkad, with an institution teaching satirical art forms.
Ambalappuzha, in Alappuzha district, is where Nambiar is believed to have first performed the thullal at the Sri Krishna temple, and where he died.

history.what: Kunchan Nambiar is born, per Wikipedia.
Ottamthullal is introduced, traditionally credited to him.
Nambiar moves to the court of Marthanda Varma.
Nambiar dies in Ambalappuzha.
Competitions are held, and the form is staged with women soloists and with groups.

future: Keep teaching the recitation style and rhythm to young performers.
Support schools and youth festivals that stage thullal competitions.
Publish clean, annotated texts of the stories with the satire explained.
Pay senior performers who teach.
Record performances and the chorus responses on video.

name: Pandavani
tagline: One singer, one tambura and the Mahabharata, with Bhima as the hero.
facts: Form: sung and acted telling of the Mahabharata
Two styles: Vedamati (seated) and Kapalik (improvised, standing)
Instrument: tambura or ektara, often with kartal
Traditionally performed by men; women began in the 1980s
art: Pandavani is a folk form from Chhattisgarh that tells episodes of the Mahabharata through song and acting. The name means the tale of the Pandavas. In this telling Bhima, the strongest brother, is the hero.

The lead singer stands or sits with a tambura (ektara), sometimes with small bells and peacock feathers on it, and sometimes with a pair of kartal cymbals. The tambura also becomes a prop. In performance it can stand for Bhima's mace or Arjuna's bow. There are no sets. Behind the lead, a few singers sing refrains and add comments, and a harmonium and tabla or dholak may play.

Wikipedia describes two styles. In Vedamati, the singer follows a text, the Chhattisgarhi Mahabharat written in doha-chaupai metre by Sabal Singh Chauhan, and usually narrates seated. In Kapalik, the singer improvises on episodes and characters, acts out the roles, and stands and moves. Popular episodes include Draupadi's disrobing (Draupadi Cheerharan), Dushasana's death and the battle of Bhishma and Arjuna.
Nobody knows how old Pandavani is. Teejan Bai believed that it could be as old as the epic, since stories were passed on by mouth when few people could read. We do not have a documented date.
artist: Teejan Bai is the best-known name in Pandavani. She was born in 1956 in Ganiyari village near Bhilai, to a Pardhi family. As a child she heard her maternal grandfather, Brijlal Pardhi, recite the Mahabharata in Chhattisgarhi, and she began to learn. Reports name Umed Singh Deshmukh as her teacher. At 13 she gave her first public performance, in Chandrakhuri village, in the standing Kapalik style, which was unusual for a woman then.

The theatre director Habib Tanvir noticed her, and she went on to perform in Delhi and abroad, including in England, France, Germany, Turkey and Mauritius. She also performed Mahabharata scenes in Shyam Benegal's television series Bharat Ek Khoj. Her honours include the Padma Shri (1988; one source says 1987), the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1995; some sources say 1996), the Padma Bhushan (2003), the Fukuoka Prize (2018) and the Padma Vibhushan (2019).

Others carry the form. Jhaduram Devangan is named with the Vedamati style. Ritu Verma, who grew up in a Bhilai settlement and began training as a child, is among the Kapalik singers. Wikipedia lists Usha Barle, a Padma Shri awardee, among the Kapalik exponents.
place: Pandavani is sung across Chhattisgarh and in neighbouring parts of Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. Teejan Bai's own story is tied to the Durg and Bhilai area, a region of villages beside the steel city.
Any open space is a stage. In villages that can mean a courtyard or a festival ground, and the singer's voice carries the story to the back of the crowd.

history.what: The origin of Pandavani is not documented. Teejan Bai believed it could be as old as the epic.
Performance was by men, in village settings.
Teejan Bai is born near Bhilai (date of birth is given differently by sources).
At 13, Teejan Bai gives her first public performance at Chandrakhuri in the Kapalik style.
Women begin to perform Pandavani, according to Wikipedia. Teejan Bai tours abroad.
Teejan Bai receives the Padma Shri, the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, the Padma Bhushan (2003) and the Padma Vibhushan (2019).
She receives the Fukuoka Prize.

future: Fund apprenticeships so girls and boys can learn both Vedamati and Kapalik from living singers, not only from recordings.
Pay fair fees for village and festival shows, so a singer can live on the art.
Record full multi-hour performances with the singers' own commentary, and keep them in an open archive.
Document the Chhattisgarhi Mahabharat text and the singers' improvised episodes side by side.
Support the women who followed Teejan Bai, and the musicians who play behind the lead singer.

name: Ramlila
tagline: The Ramayana told in song and speech over ten or more nights, with the whole town as audience.
facts: UNESCO-inscribed in 2008 (first proclaimed in 2005)
Based on Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas
Performed around Dussehra, usually over ten to twelve days
Ramnagar's version runs for about a month
art: Ramlila means Rama's play. It is a staged telling of the Ramayana in scenes, with song, narration, recitation and dialogue. UNESCO says it is based on the Ramcharitmanas, the Awadhi poem of the sixteenth-century poet Tulsidas, and builds to the battle of Rama and Ravana.

It is performed in the autumn around Dussehra, the festival that celebrates Rama's return from exile. UNESCO says most Ramlilas last ten to twelve days, and that Ramnagar's can last a month. In many towns the story ends with the burning of giant effigies of Ravana on Vijayadashami night, though the size and style differ.

UNESCO says each scene builds to a high point marked by a sequence of icons. The audience may sing along. UNESCO describes the performance as one that draws in the whole community regardless of caste, religion or age.

Ramnagar's version is staged in the open town, with different parts of the story played in different spots across the town. The audience walks from one location to the next. The sets are not stage painting but real places that stand for Ayodhya, Lanka and the forest.
Wikipedia says the actors who embody the characters are called svarup, a word meaning divine embodiment, and that they are chosen from local actors.
artist: Most Ramlilas are run by local committees, called samitis, funded by neighbourhoods. Villagers take part for free, acting or making masks, costumes, make-up, effigies and lights, according to UNESCO.

Actors for the main roles are chosen locally. Wikipedia says that some roles are handed down within families. In Ramnagar, Wikipedia says the Kashi Naresh, the head of the former ruling house of Benares, opens the festivities. I did not find a named list of performers I could confirm.
Backstage are the makers of effigies and masks, tailors, lamp keepers, singers, and the reciters who chant the Ramcharitmanas. Their work is mostly unpaid or modestly paid.
Our approach: ask each committee how its Ramlila is run, who plays which role, and who keeps the craft skills, and let them tell it in their words.
place: Ramlila is performed mainly in the Hindi belt of north India. UNESCO names Ayodhya, Ramnagar, Benares, Vrindavan, Almora, Satna and Madhubani as especially representative places. Delhi has large Ramlila grounds, including Ramlila Maidan.

Ramnagar is a town across the Ganga from Varanasi, with the fort of the former rulers of Benares. Its Ramlila uses the whole town and the fields around it. Wikipedia says the plays are held every evening for 31 days.
The autumn setting matters. Dussehra comes after the monsoon, in the Navaratri season, and Ramlila grounds across north India fill with fairs and food stalls.

history.what: Wikipedia says Ramlila-like performances existed before 1625 and that the first productions are not documented.
Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi. UNESCO says it made the epic reachable to ordinary people and that most Ramlilas use it.
Tradition says Tulsidas's student Megha Bhagat started the Ramcharitmanas-based Ramlila in this year. Historians have not confirmed it.

Maharaja Udit Narayan Singh of Benares is said to have begun the Ramnagar Ramlila. Most sources give about 1830, though some give other dates and local legends differ. A popular story says he missed a Ramlila at another town and was advised to start one at Ramnagar.
Later patrons of Ramnagar, including his successor Ishwari Narayan Singh, are credited in some accounts with giving the staging its present form.
UNESCO proclaimed Ramlila in 2005 as a Masterpiece, and in 2008 it was inscribed on the Representative List.
UNESCO notes that television and mass media have drawn audiences away. Ramlila continues in hundreds of towns and villages, with Ramnagar still supported by the former royal family.

future: Support the committees and village groups that stage Ramlila with small grants for costumes, lights and sound.
Write down the full texts, tunes and stage directions of each place, with the reciters credited by name.
Give mask, effigy and costume makers fair pay and a share of festival income.
Document Ramnagar's staging with maps, audio and film, in Hindi and English, and keep copies in the community.
Open roles carefully, with the committees' consent, to girls and to people from groups that have not taken part.
Improve safety and sanitation for large crowds and burning effigies, and reduce waste.

name: Ramman
tagline: A village in the Garhwal Himalaya stages the Rama story in wooden masks for its guardian god.
facts: Form: ritual theatre with masks, song and drum
Held at Saloor-Dungra, Chamoli district, in April-May
For the village deity Bhumiyal Devta
UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2009
art: Ramman is a religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal Himalaya. UNESCO describes it as a mix of the recitation of a version of the Rama epic and other legends, songs, masked dances, music and historical re-enactments.

The festival is held for Bhumiyal Devta, the village guardian god. Wikipedia says the date is set by the village priest and falls after Baisakhi, and that it runs for about ten days, though another passage gives a longer span. The god tours the village and performances take place in the temple courtyard.

The programme includes an invocation to Ganesha, a sun dance, dances of buffalo herders and a trader couple, the Ramkatha episodes from Rama's visit to Janakpur to his coronation, and a comic Maal dance on a Gurkha-Garhwali battle. It ends with a feast of the god's prasada.

Masks are central. Wikipedia says they are carved from the stem of the bhoj tree (Betula utilis). The Tribune reported in 2009 that makers traditionally also used walnut or madar wood, picked on an auspicious day.
artist: UNESCO says the festival is organised by the villagers, and each caste and occupational group has its own role. Brahmins lead prayers and rituals. Only the Bhandaris, who are Kshatriya, may wear the most sacred mask, that of Narasimha, the half-man, half-lion deity. The family hosting the god through the year keeps a strict daily routine.

Wikipedia adds that Jagaris, bards who sing the Jagar, and drummers from the Das community have key parts. All households take part, and the Das drummers are given raised status during the performance.
The Tribune warned in 2009 that few people still knew mask-making, and that masks had been stolen from several villages in Chamoli. I found no later report that says how this has changed.
place: Saloor-Dungra are twin villages in the Painkhanda valley of Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. The festival is held in late April, in the high-hill spring after winter.

The Tribune says similar masked Ramayana performances are held in other villages in Chamoli and Rudraprayag districts, each with its own local deity. The Saloor-Dungra version is the one UNESCO lists.

history.what: One passage in Wikipedia says the festival has been held for roughly 500 years. No dated source is given.
The writer Nand Kishore Hatwal, quoted in the Tribune, suggests the masks may have been inspired by Chhau of Assam and Bengal, brought by traders. This is a view, not settled.
The Tribune reports that 21 masks were stolen from the village of Lata in Chamoli.
Wikipedia says the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts introduced Ramman to a wider audience.
UNESCO inscribed Ramman on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (decision 4.COM 13.43).
Wikipedia says Ramman was shown in India's Republic Day parade.

future: Training: pass on mask carving and the Jagar songs to young people in the village, with the elders teaching.
Livelihood: give the Das drummers, Jagaris and mask makers fair payment and a share of any visitor income.
Materials: protect the bhoj and other trees used for masks, and carve replacement masks.
Documentation: photograph and record every mask, its name and its role, and keep copies in the village.
Protection: keep the masks safe, and keep the festival a village ritual and not a stage show.

name: Saang
tagline: Open-air folk theatre where men play every role and the story is sung in raagni.
facts: Form: folk theatre of song, dialogue and mimicry
Name: from swang, meaning imitation
Sung in Haryanvi raagni style
Traditionally played by men, including women's roles
art: Saang, also spelt Swang, is a folk theatre of Haryana. The name is said to come from swang, meaning to imitate: to take on the form, dress, behaviour and speech of another person. It mixes story, song, dialogue and some dance.

Wikipedia describes a troupe of about ten to twelve performers working in an open space or on a simple platform, without backdrops, curtains or microphones. A performance can last five or six hours. A comic character, the makhaulia, is part of the show, and much of the dialogue is improvised. Singing in the Haryanvi raagni style is at the centre.

The stories come from the Puranas, the Mahabharata and folk tales. The Tribune notes that Lakhmi Chand's raagnis were also written on Vedanta and on love and separation. Titles named in the sources include Raja Harishchandra, Heer Ranjha, Meera Bai, Jani Chor, Nal-Damayanti, Raja Bhoj and Raja Gopichand. Plays usually end with good defeating evil.

The Tribune records that some critics have objected to coarse content in some performances. It also says Saang has been used for entertainment and for raising money for village amenities. Newer productions have taken up themes such as health, literacy and women's empowerment, according to Wikipedia.
artist: Sources name a line of Saang poet-performers. Wikipedia lists six major folk poets: Deep Chand Bahman, Lakhmi Chand, Jat Mehar Singh, Baje Bhagat, Mange Ram and Ramkishan Vyas. The Tribune adds Sheki Ram and Tule Ram, Lakhmi Chand's son.

Deep Chand of Sonipat is described as a patwari by profession who gave the form new dimensions. The Tribune says he was given the title Rai Sahib. Wikipedia gives his years as 1884-1940. Ali Bux of Rewari is named by Wikipedia as an early pioneer.

Men traditionally played all the roles, including women. Wikipedia names Dr Sandhya Sharma as a woman performer who works with Satish Kashyap's troupe, which it describes as a surviving company that has performed at the National School of Drama and elsewhere. These are Wikipedia's claims, which the page itself marks as needing better citations.
place: Wikipedia places Saang in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh, and says Nautanki and Tamasha grew from the same swang traditions. This page focuses on Haryana.

The sources tie the main names to particular towns: Sonipat for Deep Chand and Lakhmi Chand, Rewari for Ali Bux, and Narnaund for Ramkishan Vyas. Performances were held in village squares and open grounds, often at fairs and festivals.

history.what: The Tribune quotes the poet Mange Ram as crediting Krishan Lal with first scripting and performing Saang in 1750. Wikipedia says tradition credits Kishan Lal Bhaat about 200 years ago and also gives a rival view naming Kavi Shankar Das of Meerut. Both pages also name Ali Bux. Sources differ.
The Tribune says the early form resembled a mujra, with men in all roles. Wikipedia says it had two strands, Kirtan style and Nautanki style.
Wikipedia gives these as Ali Bux's years. It says Deep Chand polished his style, adding music, dance, mime and ballad recitation.
Deep Chand Bahman's years, as given by Wikipedia.
Lakhmi Chand's years, as given by Wikipedia. The Tribune calls him the founder of the present raagni form.
Tule Ram, Lakhmi Chand's son, who worked to keep his father's work alive, according to the Tribune. It says instruments, postures and length of shows changed over time.
Wikipedia notes a proscenium production of Jani Chor in 1999 and Manish Joshi Bismil's Lakhmiprem in 2012, as part of efforts to bring Saang to new audiences.

future: Documentation: record full performances with the poets' texts, and write down the names of makhaulia, singers and musicians who rarely appear in print.
Training: support troupes that teach young people the singing and mimicry, including girls and women, where the community agrees.
Livelihood: pay fair fees for festival and school performances, and for work on health and literacy themes.
Texts: gather and publish the poets' scripts with Haryanvi originals and plain Hindi or English notes, naming each poet.
Protection: Wikipedia calls the form endangered. Local archives and universities in Haryana could hold the recordings.

name: Tamasha
tagline: Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre of song, dance, jokes and sharp commentary.
facts: Form: folk theatre mixing song, dance, skit and comedy
Two types: sangeet bari and dholki bari
Stock roles: shahir, songadya, nachya, dholkya
About 450 troupes with roughly 10,000 artists in 2002, per Wikipedia
art: Tamasha is a folk theatre of Maharashtra that combines song, dance, drama and comedy. The word is of Persian origin and means a show. Wikipedia names two main types: the older sangeet bari, with more music and dance, and dholki bari, which has more drama.

Shailaja Paik describes a standard opening: gan (a prayer to Ganesh), a salutation to the audience, gaulan (a playful scene with Krishna and the milkmaids), batavani (comic talk), savaljavab (a question-and-answer contest) and then the vag, a skit.

The cast has stock roles. Paik lists the sardar who leads the talk, the songadya the jester, the dancers (nachya or nachi), the dholkya who plays the drum, and the chorus. Lavani, the song form with gesture, is part of tamasha. Wikipedia says tamasha has been used to talk about caste and politics, including by the Satyashodhak Samaj.
artist: Tamasha has long been carried by performers from communities that were placed low in the caste order. Paik, a historian, says that travelling artists came largely from Kolhati and other wandering castes, and she quotes the folklorist Balwant Gargi as saying Mahars and Mangs were the first to perform it. Wikipedia says the traditional practitioners came from castes labelled low.

Paik also shows how the art was judged. She argues that late colonial and upper-caste opinion labelled tamasha ashlil, meaning vulgar, a stigma that stuck to Dalit performers, while after the state of Maharashtra was formed the same form was praised as authentic folk culture. Women performers have been central, especially of lavani. The Vithabai Narayangaonkar Lifetime Achievement Award, named by Wikipedia, honours a leading performer.
Our approach: name the troupe owners and women performers, and place the art in its caste history without stereotype.
place: Tamasha is found across rural Maharashtra, performed by travelling troupes who move between village fairs. Wikipedia says that after Independence, urban audiences turned away from folk forms and tamasha stayed mainly in the countryside.

Paik links its courtly phase to Pune, where the Peshwas patronised lavani and tamasha in the 18th century. Wikipedia mentions an early reference to theatrical entertainment in the Nashik cave inscriptions of the Satavahana period, but treat that as a loose link rather than a direct line.

history.what: Paik notes mentions of lavani sung by women of Dom and Mang castes in medieval texts, and village performers paid in cash and kind.
Under the Peshwas, tamasha and lavani become court entertainment, Paik says. Wikipedia says tamasha took its distinct form in the late Peshwa period.
The Peshwa is defeated by the British. Paik says traders, landlords and ordinary people then sustained the performers.
Tamasha is labelled vulgar, according to Paik.
Paik says the new state and upper castes began to promote tamasha as authentic folk culture.
Pinjra, a Marathi film set in the tamasha world, is released (Wikipedia).
Wikipedia reports about 450 troupes with roughly 10,000 artists.

future: Training: support young performers and musicians within troupes, and pay senior artists to teach.
Livelihood: steady bookings and fair pay, and protection for women performers.
Materials: help small troupes with sound, costume and transport.
Documentation: record scripts, songs and the stories of performers with their consent.
Protection: treat performers with dignity, and challenge the old stigma.

name: Therukoothu
tagline: Street theatre of the Tamil villages, often telling the Mahabharata and Draupadi's story overnight.
facts: Name means street play (theru, street; koothu, play)
Often linked to festivals for the goddess Draupadi Amman
Performed overnight, in a village open space
Kattaikkuttu is a closely related form, with a different history of the name
art: Therukoothu, also spelled Terukkuttu, is a folk theatre of northern Tamil Nadu. It is performed in the open air, usually at night, with a mix of song, dance, speech and acting. Many plays come from the Mahabharata, and Draupadi is central.

Draupadi is also worshipped as a goddess, Draupadi Amman. Scholars write about village festivals for her in which the Mahabharata is told over several nights, in some places ten. Performances of core episodes include Draupadi's marriage and the disrobing of Draupadi. Other stories include the dice game.

The actors wear bold face paint, wide skirts, anklets and heavy wooden headgear and shoulder ornaments, which mark royal and divine characters. The wooden pieces are called kattai in Wikipedia's account of Kattaikkuttu.

A narrator and clown figure, the kattiyakaran, introduces scenes and connects them to the audience. Singing and live music carry the story. The Kattaikkuttu Sangam is also known for keeping alive the mukavinai, an instrument covered in The News Minute.

A note on the names. Wikipedia says Terukkuttu and Kattaikkuttu are often used for the same thing today, but historically they could mean different things. Terukkuttu referred to short mobile shows by two actors in a procession for the goddess Mariamman. Kattaikkuttu refers to overnight shows at a fixed place with an ensemble of about fifteen actors and musicians. Local usage varies.
artist: Performers are called koothar. They were traditionally men, who took the women's roles too. Wikipedia says women have joined in modern times. The Kattaikkuttu Sangam opened training to rural girls and has an all-girls ensemble.

Training is under a teacher, called a nattuvanar, in a workshop called a koothu pattarai, according to Wikipedia's article on koothu. Many performers are farmers or labourers who perform in the festival season.

One name widely associated with Purisai is Kannappa Thambiran, who is described as a leading figure of the form. A source says he received the Kalaimamani title from the Tamil Nadu Eyal Isai Nataka Mandram in 1972. After his death in 2003, his sons began the annual Purisai festival, according to a theatre report, and the troupe has run a school since 2007.

In Punjarasantankal near Kanchipuram, the Kattaikkuttu Sangam was founded by the actor and director P. Rajagopal and the Dutch scholar Hanne M. de Bruin. The Kattaikkuttu Gurukulam, a school for children, began there in 2002. Dr de Bruin has written books on the form.
place: Therukoothu belongs to the north of Tamil Nadu, around Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Kanchipuram. Purisai is a village between Cheyyar and Vandavasi in Tiruvannamalai district, about 120 km from Chennai, known as a centre of the form.
Draupadi temples dot the villages of this region, and their annual festivals are the main occasions for shows. A single Mahabharata may take many nights, with the audience sleeping on the ground.

The performance space is a village street or open yard, lit by lamps, today often by electric lights. Shows follow the farming calendar and the temple festival season. Wikipedia says that during the Covid-19 lockdowns the form suffered when festivals stopped.

history.what: Wikipedia says koothu has been practised in Tamil Nadu since the Sangam period. Scholars do not agree on how directly today's forms connect with that older koothu.
Mahabharata festivals for Draupadi grew in the Tamil north. Sources I consulted give no clear timeline.
Kannappa Thambiran of Purisai received the Kalaimamani title, according to one source.
One account dates the registration of the Kattaikkuttu Sangam to 1 November 1990. Another says its founder started it in 2002, so the date is uncertain.
The Kattaikkuttu Gurukulam began in Punjarasantankal as a school for rural children.
Kannappa Thambiran died. His sons carry on the Purisai festival.
The Purisai troupe began a school of Therukoothu for all ages.
Covid-19 lockdowns stopped the festival season, and Wikipedia says the Gurukulam closed in March 2020.

future: Support village troupes with year-round work, health cover and fair fees from temple committees.
Back schools like those in Purisai and Punjarasantankal, with funding for children from farm and labourer families.
Record whole overnight plays, the songs and the clown's lines, in Tamil, with subtitles and notes in English.
Make wooden headgear and costume making a recognised trade with apprentices and fair prices.
Open more places for girls and women, working with senior performers.
Help visitors find real village performances, with clear information and fair payment to the troupes.

name: Tholpavakoothu
tagline: Leather shadow puppets tell the Ramayana to a goddess, in a temple theatre, by lamplight.
facts: Form: ritual shadow puppetry in Bhadrakali (Bhagavathy) temples
Text: verses based on Kamban's Tamil Ramayana
Stage: the koothumadam, a theatre beside the temple
Season: roughly January to May
art: Tholpavakoothu means leather (thol), puppet (pava) and play (koothu). Flat leather puppets are held between a lamp and a white screen, and their shadows tell the story of the Ramayana. It is part of the worship of the goddess Bhadrakali, in Bhadrakali or Bhagavathy temples.

The puppetry.org.in text says the story runs from Rama's birth to his coronation, in 21 parts over 21 evenings. Devotees say Bhadrakali was away killing the demon Darika and missed the battle of Rama and Ravana, so it is staged for her. An Al Jazeera report says her image is placed in front of the stage.

The verses are called koothu-kavikal. They draw heavily on Kamban's Tamil Ramayana, though performers have changed some and added their own. Prose and talk are in a mix of Tamil and Malayalam. Al Jazeera reports that performers learn about 2,100 verses with their meanings. The text has been handed from teacher to student, and palm-leaf manuscripts are kept in puppeteers' homes.

Al Jazeera describes about 160 puppets for roughly 70 characters, each around 80 cm tall, made of buffalo hide and deerskin, painted with vegetable dyes and fixed to sticks. Puppetry.org.in notes that palm-leaf puppets were used long ago under the older name ola-pava-koothu, but have disappeared.
The Pulavar, the lead performer, sings, speaks and also moves the puppets. A full show also has singers, storytellers and helpers, about ten people in all according to Al Jazeera.
artist: Pulavar means scholar or teacher, and it is also the family name of the main performing families. Puppetry.org.in says a Pulavar must know the Ramayana well, along with the Puranas and shastras, and speak with ease on many subjects. The same source says the art is performed today by members of the Vallalachetty and Nair communities.

Every show opens with a prayer to teachers. For five generations, puppeteers have named Kuzhiyathu Kandappezhuthachan first, then Venmaya Pulavar, then Chinnathampi Vadhyar. The same source credits Chinnathampi Vadhyar, about 350 years ago by its estimate, with bringing Kamban's verses into the form.

Krishnankutty Pulavar of Koonathara, near Shoranur, is remembered as a leading master. Wikipedia lists him as a Sangeet Natak Akademi awardee, but I did not find the year. Kerala Tourism lists a memorial centre in his name at Koonathara. His son K. K. Ramachandra Pulavar was named a Padma Shri in 2021, as reported by press and Wikipedia. His grandson Rajeev Pulavar is reported to have received the Sangeet Natak Akademi's Bismillah Khan Yuva Puraskar in 2016. I did not check the Akademi list for these awards.

Al Jazeera reports on another Palakkad family which has performed for eight generations and covers 82 temples. It runs a school that teaches children and adults. The family said income fell sharply in the pandemic and that young people were less interested. They now also offer workshops and rent or sell puppets. Women performers are not mentioned in the sources I read.
place: Tholpavakoothu is found in Palakkad and Thrissur districts and nearby villages, along the Bharathapuzha river and the Palakkad gap, where Kerala meets the Tamil country. That is why the language of the text mixes Tamil and Malayalam.

The setting is the koothumadam, a special theatre built within or beside the temple. Al Jazeera describes a stage of about 42 feet, lit from behind by lamps. Shows are held mainly between January and May, in the time of temple festivals. Al Jazeera notes that a full cycle can run about 21 days around the Pooram festival in April, while shorter shows can last about thirty minutes.

The materials come from the village economy. Hides come from animals killed for other reasons, vegetable dyes colour the leather and the lamps burn oil or, now, bulbs. Sources I read do not say exactly where hides are bought today.

Koonathara, near Shoranur, and the Palakkad area around it are the best-known centres for visitors and learners. Palakkad's District Heritage Museum has also shown a robot-operated puppet prototype from a Thrissur company, Inker Robotics. The Pulavars told Al Jazeera that they use robots only for stage shows, not temple rituals.

history.what: Puppetry.org.in says the origins are ancient and no founder or author can be named.
The form was already performed in Bhadrakali temples before Kamba Ramayana became popular in Kerala, according to puppetry.org.in.
Chinnathampi Vadhyar brings Kamban's verses into the performance, which makes it more popular. Scholars also differ on Kamban's own date; some sources say 12th century.
Al Jazeera quotes a figure of roughly 300 years for one family's tradition.
The poet Kunjan Nambiar praised the art in his work Ghoshayatra, according to puppetry.org.in.
Members of the Koonathara family receive national honours, per press reports and Wikipedia.
The pandemic halts shows and cuts income, as reported by Al Jazeera.
Robot-operated puppets are tested for museum display in Palakkad.

future: Fund apprenticeships so that young people can learn the 2,100 verses, puppet cutting and temple singing from senior Pulavars.
Give puppet makers and hide workers a fair, regular supply of good leather, and look at alternatives that keep the shadow quality.
Record whole 21-night cycles with Malayalam and English notes, and digitise the palm-leaf manuscripts with the families' consent.
Keep the temple ritual in the temple and design separate, shorter shows for stage and school audiences.
Offer health cover and pensions for senior Pulavars, since income is seasonal.
Support women and children from the Pulavar villages to learn, if the families wish.

name: Tholu Bommalata
tagline: Tall, jointed leather puppets, lit from behind, telling the Ramayana through the night.
facts: Form: Telugu shadow puppet theatre
Puppets: 120 to 180 cm tall, jointed, made of treated hide
Main story: the Ramayana, after Ranganatha's Telugu text
Troupes are family-based
art: Tholu Bommalata means the play of leather puppets. Sahapedia describes it as the shadow theatre of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and parts of Karnataka. The puppets are large, between 120 and 180 cm, and are jointed at the arms, legs, head and neck. Most show the face in profile.

Skins are soaked, scraped, stretched, dried and beaten until they are translucent. The figure is outlined, cut out, pierced with chisels for decoration and painted. Colour follows convention: Rama and Krishna are blue, and women are yellow or orange. Sahapedia notes that natural dyes have often given way to industrial paint.

A show opens with a prayer to Ganesha and a dance by Saraswathi, then comic skits by jesters, then the main epic. The repertoire is mostly the Ramayana, using the 16th-century Telugu text by Ranganatha, with some Mahabharata and Bhagavata stories.
The puppets are held against a white cloth screen lit from behind. Puppeteers sing and speak for the characters, and live music with drums, harmonium, cymbals and a mukhaveena goes with them.
artist: Troupes are made up of family members, with five to ten people and usually three or four main performers. The head is called the bhagavatar or sutradhar. Skills pass from father to son, and children begin as toddlers.
Sahapedia says many troupes come from families that migrated from Maharashtra, probably around the 17th century, and some still speak a form of Marathi at home while performing in Telugu.

Puppeteers have also been makers of the puppets. Sources here do not agree about the animal skins used, and Sahapedia says traditional rules about which hide is used for which figure are often ignored now.
place: Nimmalakunta village in Anantapur district (now Sri Sathya Sai district) is the best known centre for making the puppets, and Wikipedia says puppets and accessories are made there today.
Performances were traditionally held outdoors at night, for example at festivals near temples such as the Shivaratri night. Today shows usually last about two hours.

history.what: Sahapedia says shadow puppetry was popular in South India by the 4th to 6th centuries CE. Wikipedia places it earlier, in the Satavahana period, and links it to Southeast Asian shadow theatre. Scholars do not agree on these origins.
Ranganatha's Telugu Ramayana, the text most used in shows, dates to this period according to Sahapedia.
Many puppeteer families are said to have come from Maharashtra.
Sahapedia describes a decline as films spread and patronage ended. Troupes took up other work to survive.
Some families still perform. Others make lamps, home decor and other crafts from leather for sale.

future: Pay troupes to perform in villages and schools, so the art has regular work and new audiences.
Record full night-long performances with the senior puppeteers, with Telugu and English notes.
Support makers who still use natural dyes and traditional hide, and pay them fairly for it.
Teach children from performing families alongside school, so learning the art is not a choice against education.
Keep puppets in museums and show how they are made, while keeping new puppets in use on the screen.

name: Togalu Gombeyatta
tagline: A play of leather dolls: coloured hide figures dance as shadows, with epic tales sung from behind the screen.
facts: Form: shadow puppetry with flat leather figures
Name: togalu (leather), gombe (doll), ata (play)
Stories: Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata
Puppet size: from about 6 inches to 4 feet
art: Togalu gombeyatta means a play of leather dolls in Kannada. It is the shadow puppetry of Karnataka. The puppets are flat, jointed figures of leather, held against a lit cloth screen so that the audience sees coloured shadows.

Wikipedia says the figures range from about 4 by 3 feet down to 6 by 3 inches, and are made of goat hide and deerskin because they are translucent and take dye well. Other sources say buffalo, goat or sheep hide, and note that deerskin is no longer used because deer cannot be killed. The hide is cleaned and treated, drawn on, painted with vegetable dyes, cut and punched with fine holes for detail. A bindugopalrao.com interview with a puppeteer says the hide is washed until almost white.

Limbs are loosely joined so that they move apart. A stick runs up the middle of the figure, and single strings control special movements. The puppeteer sits behind the screen, speaks and sings the parts, and music comes from a harmonium or a mouth veena (mukha-veena), according to Wikipedia. Traditionally an oil lamp lit the screen. Low-voltage bulbs have replaced it in many places.

The stories come from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata, together with folk tales. The puppeteer interviewed says Hanuman is a favourite. Shows were traditionally held at night, in a space outside the village or in a temple courtyard, and could go on until dawn.
artist: Wikipedia does not name the community of puppeteers. A puppeteer family from Ramanagara district, interviewed on bindugopalrao.com, belongs to the Killekyatha community, and the article says the puppeteers are called gomberamas. It adds that they are said to be originally Marathi and descended from people who came with Maratha soldiers; they speak a mix of Marathi and Kannada. This is the community's own account and I could not check it elsewhere.

The same article names Kalaviduru Gowramma of Ramanagara as a puppeteer, who says about 10,000 practitioners are spread over Ballari, Tumakuru, Gubbi and Nagamangala. I could not confirm that figure from another source. She says a single puppet can cost close to Rs 10,000.

Anupama Hoskere of Dhaatu Puppet Theatre, Bengaluru, is named in the same article as helping bring rural puppeteers to city audiences. Deccan Herald reports a revival at G. B. Saragur village, Mysuru district. I could not open that report to read details.
The same art is known by other names and kept by other communities in nearby states: tolu bommalata in Andhra Pradesh, tolu bommalattam in Tamil Nadu and tolpavakoothu in Kerala.
place: Karnataka is the main home of togalu gombeyatta. Sources name Ramanagara district, southern Mysuru, Ballari, Tumakuru, Gubbi and Nagamangala. I looked for Koppal and Anantapur and found no source for them, so they are not claimed here.

Wikipedia gives a long history for the region: royal support from the 2nd century, flowering under the Rashtrakutas (10th century) and the Vijayanagara Empire (15th century), and changes in ornament under the Bahmani kingdom. After the Bahmani decline, patronage shrank and shows moved to villages and temples. This is a general summary and individual dates should be checked.

The puppets are made of leather from village animals and coloured with local plant dyes. The interview names Bhadravati as a source of paint. Because shows are at night and outdoors, the art fits village fairs and temple festivals. I could not verify a link to the Dasara festival in any source, so none is claimed.
Today the Karnataka Chitrakala Parishat in Bengaluru has studied the art and holds a good collection of leather puppets, according to Wikipedia.

history.what: Wikipedia places shadow puppetry in the region in ancient times, with royal patronage recorded from the 2nd century. I could not verify this against a primary record.
The art is said to flourish under the Rashtrakutas and to spread into Odisha and Maharashtra.
The Vijayanagara Empire is described as the peak of its patronage.
Turkish influence is said to have changed puppet ornament; patronage shrinks after the Bahmani decline.
Shows move to villages and temple complexes; the sources I read give no clear dates.
Steel stage frames, loudspeakers and electric light come in, according to Wikipedia.
Groups such as Dhaatu Puppet Theatre in Bengaluru help bring puppeteers to wider audiences; a revival at G. B. Saragur is reported.

future: Bring puppeteer families into schools as paid teachers, so children learn drawing, hide cutting and singing.
Help families buy hide, dyes and tools in bulk and sell puppets at fair prices through a cooperative.
Record full epic nights with the singers and keep the verses in Kannada and Marathi-Kannada speech as performed.
Map which villages in Ballari, Tumakuru, Ramanagara, Mysuru and nearby districts still have working troupes, and do a proper survey of numbers.
Keep the old open-air night shows alive at fairs while adding shorter city shows.
Look at a GI or other recognition with the families' consent.

name: Yakshagana
tagline: Night-long stage epics with tall crowns, bright faces, drums and a singer who leads the story.
facts: Region: coastal Karnataka and Kasaragod, Kerala
Two styles: Tenku (south) and Badagu (north)
Performed from dusk to dawn in the traditional form
Season runs roughly from November to May
art: Yakshagana is a stage form that joins dance, music, dialogue, costume and make-up. It is performed in coastal Karnataka and in Kasaragod district of Kerala. Traditionally it runs from dusk to dawn, with stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata and other Hindu and Jain sources.

A group of musicians, the himmela, sits at the side and is led by the bhagavata, who sings and narrates. The actors, called the mummela, dance and speak their lines. Instruments include the maddale and chande drums, the harmonium and finger cymbals. Wikipedia notes that dialogue and much of the performance are improvised on the day within the story.

The two main styles are named by region. Tenkutittu is found from Dakshina Kannada to Kasaragod, and Wikipedia describes it as showing Carnatic music influence and as known for spins, jumps and big demon roles. Badagutittu is found from Udupi northwards to Uttara Kannada and puts more weight on facial expression and dialogue. Local people may describe the difference differently.

The costume is bold. There are tall crowns (kirita and pagade), ornaments for the chest and arms, and wide dress padding. Ornaments were traditionally made of light wood with gold foil and mirror work. Wikipedia says the most elaborate make-up, for demons, can take three to four hours to apply.
A show often opens with drumming and ends with a prayer to Ganesha.
artist: Yakshagana artists are trained by gurus from the age when they are young, in dance, speech and the story. Wikipedia names the Srimaya Yakshagana Kalakendra at Gunavante, founded by Keremane Shambhu Hegde, as a residential school of the gurukula type, and the Yakshagana Kalakendra at the Govinda Pai Research Institute in Udupi as another training centre.

Most of the work is done by troupes, called melas. Wikipedia lists well-known ones, such as the Dharmasthala, Kateel, Idugunji, Mandarthi and Perdoor melas. Some are temple troupes that tour the coast during the season, and some have tickets. It estimates around 30 professional troupes and 200 amateur ones.
Men traditionally played the female roles. Wikipedia says women now perform too. Make-up, costume making and drumming are specialised skills that also pass within families.
Our approach: name the bhagavatas, actors and costume makers in every story, and record how families and troupes train their young.
place: Yakshagana is rooted on the western coast between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. The towns most linked to it are Udupi, Mangaluru and Kasaragod, and temples such as Dharmasthala and Kateel support their own troupes.
The season runs after the monsoon and harvest, from about November to May. Troupes travel between temples and village grounds. In the dry season many villages hold open-air shows lasting all night.
Wikipedia says the troupe system and the temple festival calendar are central to its livelihood, and that some troupes now sell tickets and perform in halls.

history.what: Wikipedia credits Naraharitirtha, a disciple of Madhvacharya, with bringing Yakshagana to Udupi in the 12th century. This rests on tradition, and scholars do not agree on early dates.
The earliest written evidence cited is an inscription at Kurugodu, according to Wikipedia.
The poet Parthi Subba was already established, as Wikipedia notes.
Several well-known temple troupes trace their origins here, such as Dharmasthala and Kateel (from 1867).
Tent troupes added electric lighting and ticketed audiences, which made the art more commercial.

The writer Shivarama Karanth, born in coastal Karnataka, reworked the form. Wikipedia says he added Western instruments, cut the length from about 12 hours to under three, and staged new plots. His experiments drew criticism, and Wikipedia mentions a legal ruling limiting the use of the Yakshagana name for them. The details need to be checked.
Yakshagana is staged in villages, temples and city halls, and has training schools. Wikipedia estimates around 1,000 professional artists doing 180 to 200 shows each season.

future: Support gurukula places so children of troupe families can study Yakshagana alongside school.
Give costume, crown and make-up artists recognised training, fair pay and credit.
Record whole night-long performances from both Tenku and Badagu styles, with commentary in Kannada, Tulu and English.
Help troupes with off-season work, health cover and insurance for travel.
Build more roles for women and open training to girls, with the full support of senior gurus.
Welcome visitors with a short guide to the story and the style before the show begins.
